# Locality Research Guide: Arkansas Region — Pre-1800 (Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdictional Context

The area now called Arkansas had no independent political existence before 1800. Understanding which jurisdiction governed it at a given moment is essential to knowing where records were created and where they are now held:

| Period | Controlling Authority | Administrative Center |
|---|---|---|
| 1686–1762 | French Louisiana | New Orleans / Paris |
| 1762–1800 | Spanish Louisiana (Province of Louisiana / Provincia de Luisiana) | New Orleans / Havana |
| 1800 (Oct.) | French Louisiana (secret Treaty of San Ildefonso) | Nominal only |
| 1803 | United States — Orleans/Louisiana Territory | Washington / St. Louis |
| 1812–1819 | Missouri Territory | St. Louis |
| 1819–1836 | Arkansas Territory | Little Rock |

For the **pre-1800 Spanish period**, the only significant permanent European presence was **Arkansas Post** (established 1686, initially French), located in what is now Arkansas County. All colonial-era civil, military, and church records originate at or near that post. Researchers should treat the record trail as continuous across the 1800 handover: Spanish land grants had to be confirmed by U.S. authorities after 1803, so pre-1800 individuals often surface again in early territorial records (1803–1819).

---

## Record Survey

### 1. Sacramental Registers (Church Records)
**The single most important record class for this period.**

**FamilySearch digitized volume — browse-only, in Spanish:**
- **Image Group 008814402** — "Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)," Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, 1763–1800. **64 images.** `recordSearchablePercent: 0` (not name-indexed); `fulltextSearchable: false`. These must be browsed image-by-image. The registers are **in Spanish** — researchers must be able to read 18th-century ecclesiastical Spanish script to use them directly.

**Pre-1763 French registers (ca. 1700–1762):** French Catholic missionaries maintained sacramental registers at Arkansas Post from the early 18th century, recording baptisms, marriages, and burials of European settlers and Native Americans. These are **not on FamilySearch** as digitized images. Surviving registers are held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** and in transcribed form at the **Arkansas History Commission**. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)*

**Access summary:**
| Date range | Digitized on FamilySearch? | Indexed? | Language | Physical repository |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1763–1800 | Yes — browse-only (64 images) | No | Spanish | Arkansas History Commission; RC Diocese of Little Rock |
| ~1700–1762 | No | No | French/Latin | RC Diocese of Little Rock; Arkansas History Commission |

---

### 2. Spanish Colonial Civil and Military Records (Padrones, Censuses, Post Records)

Spain administered Arkansas Post as a military and civil outpost. Records generated include:

- **Padrones** (censuses / household lists) — periodic counts of settlers at the post, listing heads of household, family members, ages, and sometimes occupations or origins.
- **Civil post records** — correspondence, land concessions, judicial proceedings.
- **Military records** — muster rolls, pay records, officer reports for the garrison.

**FamilySearch:** No indexed collection and no digitized volume for these record types was returned by `collections_search` or `volume_search`. This is a **digitization gap** — these records exist but are not yet on FamilySearch.

**Physical repositories:**
- **Arkansas History Commission**, 1 Capitol Mall, Little Rock, AR 72201 — primary repository for state-held Spanish colonial records. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)*
- **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)**, Seville, Spain — the principal repository for all Spanish colonial administrative records in the Americas. Louisiana-era records fall under the *Papeles Procedentes de Cuba* series. Many researchers use microfilm copies without traveling to Spain.
- **Library of Congress, Manuscript Division**, Washington, DC — holds microfilm copies of Spanish colonial Louisiana records. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki ibid.)*
- **NARA** — holds some territorial-era confirmations of Spanish land grants (see Land Records below).

---

### 3. Land Records — Spanish Grants and Territorial Confirmations

Spain issued land concessions (*concesiones*) to settlers at and around Arkansas Post. After the Louisiana Purchase, the U.S. government required holders of Spanish (and French) grants to have them confirmed. This confirmation process generates a direct research bridge between pre-1800 grantees and post-1803 U.S. records.

- **Spanish concessions:** Originals at the **AGI (Seville)** and the **Arkansas History Commission**. Some transcriptions exist at the Library of Congress.
- **U.S. confirmation records (post-1803):** Claims submitted to the Board of Land Commissioners are at **NARA** and published in *American State Papers, Public Lands* (searchable via HathiTrust and other digitized sources). These documents frequently name the original Spanish grantee and the claimant together, making them invaluable for connecting colonial-era individuals to early territorial families.
- **BLM General Land Office (GLO):** Federal patents issued after U.S. surveys are at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov), but these postdate the colonial period; they reference earlier grants only incidentally.

**FamilySearch:** No pre-1800 land collection was returned. The **Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870** (Collection 2085124; 178,345 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2085124) is the earliest available Arkansas collection on FamilySearch and may include early land-owner lists or substitute sources that name individuals who received colonial-era grants.

---

### 4. French Colonial Records (Pre-1763 Background)

For ancestors present before Spanish rule (1686–1762), records were generated under French administration and are held primarily outside Arkansas:

- **Archives nationales d'outre-mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France — holds French colonial Louisiana records including censuses, notarial acts, and correspondence. Online portal: [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr).
- **Louisiana Historical Society / Louisiana State Archives** — some Louisiana-centered records covering the French Illinois Country (which included Arkansas Post) are held in New Orleans repositories.
- **Newberry Library**, Chicago — significant collection of French colonial manuscripts and maps for the Mississippi Valley.

---

### 5. Military Records — Spanish Garrison

The Arkansas Post garrison was manned by Spanish troops, sometimes rotated from New Orleans or Havana. Military service records and muster rolls are at the **AGI (Seville)**, *Papeles Procedentes de Cuba* series. Pension records for veterans of the Spanish Louisiana militia may also be at the **AGI** or at the **Archivo General Militar de Segovia**, Spain.

**FamilySearch:** No military collection for pre-1800 Arkansas was returned. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) may have some transcribed or digitized Spanish colonial militia records, but this was not confirmed by tool results.

---

### 6. Post-1800 Substitute Sources That Reach Back

Because indigenous records for the Spanish period are thin and scattered, the following early U.S.-era sources frequently document individuals whose lives began under Spanish rule:

| Collection | FamilySearch | Date range | What it captures |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870 | [Collection 2085124](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2085124) | 1819–1870 | Earliest U.S.-era population lists; may name colonial-era grantees |
| Arkansas, County Marriages, 1837–1957 | [Collection 1920452](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1920452) | 1837–1957 | First post-statehood marriages; may include older individuals born pre-1800 |
| American State Papers, Public Lands | HathiTrust / Internet Archive | 1803–1820s | Land grant confirmation claims naming original Spanish grantees |

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What it holds | Access |
|---|---|---|

## Key Researcher Warnings

- **The one digitized FamilySearch volume (008814402) is in 18th-century Spanish script, 0% name-indexed, and must be browsed image-by-image.** You cannot search it by name — you must read each of the 64 pages.

Searching "Arkansas" by name in colonial-era finding aids will fail — search "Arkansas Post," "Puesto de Arkansas," or the broader Louisiana/Cuba series.

- **The Spanish colonial records on FamilySearch cover only 1763–1800.** For the French period (1686–1762), no digitized volumes were returned — treat those years as physical/repository-only until further digitization occurs.
- **Population at Arkansas Post was tiny** — likely only a few hundred Europeans at any one time before 1800. If an ancestor is not found in these records, a negative result is meaningful: they may have arrived after 1800, or records for them may simply not survive.

# 📍 Ohio Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide
**Target Period:** c. 1780–1810 (focus: 1790, before statehood)
**Controlling Jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory → Ohio (statehood 1 March 1803)

---

## Part 1 — Jurisdictional History & Boundary Changes

### The core challenge: "Ohio" did not exist in 1790

FamilySearch's place record for Ohio carries a start date of **+1803/** — the year of statehood. Any event in 1790 occurred in the **Northwest Territory**, created by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. This distinction controls where records were created and where they are held today.

*(Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio; FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)*

### County formation — the essential first step

Before locating any record, you must determine which county held jurisdiction at the moment of the event. Counties changed rapidly and a wrong county means a blank search:

| County | Formed | Parent | Area covered in 1790 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Washington County** | 1788 | Northwest Territory | All of eastern & southeastern Ohio |
| **Hamilton County** | 1790 | Washington County | All of western Ohio |

**In 1790, only two counties existed.** Every record created that year in present-day Ohio was filed in one of these two. Subsequent splits (Ross County 1798, Adams County 1797, and dozens more through the 1810s) took territory — and future records — from these two parents. For events after 1790, trace the county lineage before searching.

*(FamilySearch wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)*

### Three competing land-survey systems (different records, different repositories)

Ohio is defined by **three wholly separate survey systems**, each generating its own record trail in a different repository:

| District | Location | Survey type | Key repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between the Scioto & Little Miami rivers (central-south Ohio) | Metes-and-bounds | **Virginia State Library, Richmond** |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio | Rectangular township grid (Connecticut Land Co.) | **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland** |
| **Congressional / BLM remainder** | Most of the rest of Ohio | Rectangular, Ordinance of 1785 | **BLM General Land Office Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) |

Identifying which district your ancestor's land fell in is a prerequisite — it determines which repository holds the surveys and warrants.

*(FamilySearch wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)*

---

## Part 2 — Records Available & Access Levels

### 🏆 1. Land Records — Best Source for 1790

Land is typically the **only** record of an individual in 1790 Ohio. Exhaust all land sources before concluding a person is unrecoverable.

**FamilySearch Collection — Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840** (ID 1542187)
- 234,567 records · 117,283 images
- Date range begins **1787** — covers the pre-statehood period directly
- ✅ **Indexed + images** (name-searchable)
- 🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187

**FamilySearch Volume — Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799** (imageGroupNumber 005112233)
- 51 images · 0% name-indexed · not full-text searchable
- ⚠️ **Browse-only** — must be examined image by image; no search shortcut exists
- Coverage: Northwest Territory, United States, 1788–1799

**BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) — federal patents for the congressional-survey portion of Ohio; free, name-searchable online; not captured in FamilySearch holdings above.

**Virginia Military District warrants & surveys** — held physically at the Virginia State Library, Richmond. Not digitized on FamilySearch for this period; requires mail request or on-site visit.

**Connecticut Western Reserve records** — Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland. Check their online catalog for digitized holdings.

---

### 2. Marriage Records

**FamilySearch Collection — Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013** (ID 1803785)
- 1,523,678 records · 761,839 images
- ✅ **Indexed + images** — begins **1789**, so it covers from the very first year of organized county government
- County clerks recorded marriage bonds and licenses from county formation onward (Washington County from 1788, Hamilton County from 1790)
- 🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785

⚠️ **Gap:** Registration was at the **county level only** — records exist only from when each county was formed. Many 1790 marriages were performed by traveling clergy with no civil record surviving at all.

---

### 3. Church Records — Vital-Records Substitute

Because no civil birth or death registration existed in 1790 Ohio (see §5), **church registers are the primary substitute** for baptisms, marriages, and burials.

**FamilySearch Collection — Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950** (ID 2246917)
- 678,234 records · 339,117 images
- ✅ **Indexed + images** — begins **1787**, pre-statehood
- 🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917

Key denominations active in 1790 Ohio: Methodist and Baptist circuit riders (throughout the Ohio Valley), Presbyterian (Washington County), Episcopal, Lutheran. Denominational archives (each denomination's national repository) hold records not yet digitized on FamilySearch.

---

### 4. Tax Records

**FamilySearch Collection — Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850** (ID 1987542)
- 345,890 records · 172,945 images · ✅ Indexed + images
- ⚠️ Begins **1800** — does **not** cover 1790. Use as a follow-on source once your ancestor is found in pre-1800 records.
- 🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542

**FamilySearch Volume — Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803** (imageGroupNumber 005112240)
- 73 images · 12% name-indexed · not full-text searchable
- 🔶 **Partially indexed** — a minority of entries are name-searchable; the majority must be browsed image by image
- Coverage: Washington County, Ohio, 1799–1803

**Tax lists function as a census substitute for 1790–1799** — they are the closest available proxy for a population listing in that gap. Tax volumes for 1790–1798 may exist on microfilm at Ohio History Connection but did not appear in FamilySearch's digitized holdings for this period.

---

### 5. Vital Records (Births & Deaths)

**Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001** (ID 1417891) — begins **1840**, fifty years after the target date. Not relevant to 1790 research; listed for completeness.

**⛔ No civil registration of births or deaths existed in Ohio in 1790** — not at the territorial, county, or local level. Church registers (§3 above) are the only systematic source for birth (baptism) and death (burial) events in this period.

---

### 6. Census Records

The **1790 federal census** was taken but **covered the Northwest Territory only partially** — most of the Ohio region was too recently settled or too unsettled for enumerators to reach. Marietta (Washington County) was enumerated; much of the territory was not.

- **1800 federal census**: First broadly useful enumeration once more counties were established.
- **1810 federal census**: First reasonably complete enumeration of Ohio as a state.

**Substitute for 1790–1799:** Use the tax records above (§4) as a population-listing proxy.

---

### 7. Military Records

Many 1790 Ohio settlers were **Revolutionary War veterans** who received bounty land in the Virginia Military District or elsewhere. Pension files are genealogically rich — they routinely contain marriage dates, children's names, wife's name, and place of origin.

- **NARA / Fold3** (fold3.com): Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants — indexed and image-searchable online
- **FamilySearch Pension Index cards**: Free, name-searchable
- The **Ohio Indian Wars of the early 1790s** (culminating in the Battle of Fallen Timbers, 1794) generated additional muster rolls and payrolls at NARA

Curated link from external_links_search: Military Records — Fold3, https://www.fold3.com/

---

### 8. Court & Probate Records

Territorial and early county court records (probate inventories, guardianship files, court minutes, naturalizations) are held at the **Ohio History Connection, Columbus** (the state archives).

⚠️ No digitized FamilySearch volumes for territorial court or probate records (1780–1810) appeared in the volume_search results — physical or microfilm research at Ohio History Connection is required. Contact: https://www.ohiohistory.org/

---

### 9. Newspapers

The *Ohio Gazette* (Marietta, 1801) was the **first newspaper in the Northwest Territory**. No newspapers existed in Ohio before 1801. After 1801, search Newspapers.com for death notices, legal notices, and land-sale advertisements.

---

### 10. Cemetery Records

Find A Grave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves index many Ohio pioneer cemeteries, including private family burying grounds — common in 1790s rural Ohio before organized church cemeteries were established. Search by county (Washington or Hamilton for 1790).

---

## Part 3 — Repository Summary

| Repository | Holds |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch — familysearch.org | Land records 1787+, marriages 1789+, church records 1787+, tax records 1800+ |
| **Ohio History Connection, Columbus** | Territorial court/probate; county deed books on microfilm |
| **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents — free, name-searchable |
| **Virginia State Library, Richmond** | Virginia Military District warrants & surveys |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland** | Connecticut Western Reserve land records |
| NARA / Fold3 | Rev. War service, pensions, bounty land, Ohio Indian Wars muster rolls |
| Find A Grave / BillionGraves | Pioneer cemetery records |
| Newspapers.com | Ohio Gazette and early newspapers (post-1801 only) |

---

## Part 4 — Honest Gap Assessment

| Gap | Nature |
|---|---|
| **No civil vital registration** in 1790 | Births and deaths were never formally recorded; church registers partially fill this — but many events went entirely unrecorded |
| **1790 federal census incomplete** for the Northwest Territory | Expect many families simply absent from the 1790 enumeration |
| **Tax records begin 1799–1800** in digital holdings | 1790–1798 tax lists may exist on microfilm at Ohio History Connection but are not in current FamilySearch digital holdings |
| **Virginia Military District & Western Reserve records** are at out-of-state physical repositories | May require mail requests or on-site visits to Richmond or Cleveland |
| **Two browse-only FamilySearch volumes** for 1788–1803 | Northwest Territory Land Records (51 images) and Washington County Tax Records (73 images) must each be reviewed image by image — budget time for manual browsing |
| **FamilySearch wiki** returned generic content only for Ohio | Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy directly for current Ohio-specific guidance |

---

## Quick-Start Strategy

1. **Pin the county first** — in 1790, only Washington County and Hamilton County existed. Every 1790 record is in one of those two.
2. **Identify the land-survey district** (Virginia Military District, Connecticut Western Reserve, or BLM congressional remainder) — this determines which out-of-state repository holds the land records.
3. **Search land records** via FamilySearch collection 1542187 (indexed) and BLM GLO — land is often the only 1790 record of an individual.
4. **Browse unindexed FamilySearch volumes** for the Northwest Territory (imageGroupNumber 005112233) and Washington County taxes 1799–1803 (imageGroupNumber 005112240) — these cannot be name-searched.
5. **Use church records** (FamilySearch collection 2246917) as your birth/death substitute.
6. **Check NARA/Fold3 pension files** — if your ancestor was a Revolutionary War veteran (very common in 1790 Ohio), the pension file may be the richest single document in your research.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** California was acquired from Mexico by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (February 1848) — gold was discovered just nine days before the treaty was signed, on January 24, 1848, at Sutter's Mill in Coloma. It was admitted as the 31st U.S. state on **September 9, 1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely.
- **County structure:** The original 27 counties were established at statehood in 1850. New counties were carved out rapidly as population surged — many Gold Rush mining communities that existed in 1852 belong to counties that had not yet been formed in 1850. Always verify which county a location belonged to in the *specific year* of your research.
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco was the dominant port and commercial hub.
- **Population:** No FamilySearch population data was returned for this fixture, but historical sources document approximately **92,000** residents in the 1850 federal census and roughly **380,000** by 1860. The influx of ~300,000 migrants during 1848–1855 made California one of the fastest-growing jurisdictions in U.S. history. (Wikipedia: *California Gold Rush*)
- **Economy:** Placer and hard-rock gold mining dominated the Mother Lode counties (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, Mariposa). Commerce, shipping, and banking concentrated in San Francisco and Sacramento.
- **Ethnic composition:** Extraordinarily diverse — Anglo-Americans from every U.S. state, Mexicans and Californios, Chileans and other Latin Americans, Chinese (arriving in large numbers from 1852), Australians ("Sydney Ducks"), French, Germans, Irish, and smaller communities from across Europe and the Pacific. Spanish-speaking Californio families predated the Rush.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (the dominant pre-Rush denomination, owing to the Mission era); Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian congregations established rapidly in mining towns; Jewish congregations in San Francisco from 1849.
- **Key events:** Discovery of gold (Jan. 24, 1848); statehood (Sept. 9, 1850); Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, 1852) targeting non-Anglo miners; decline of surface placering by mid-1850s; hydraulic and deep-shaft mining replacing '49er-style panning.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Pre-statehood (to Sept. 1850):** California was unorganized U.S. territory after the Mexican cession; records from this window are sparse and not held in any California county system.
- **1850:** 27 original counties formed simultaneously at statehood. Many later counties were partitioned from these originals throughout the 1850s (e.g., Amador from Calaveras in 1854, Plumas from Butte in 1854, Stanislaus from Tuolumne in 1854).
- **Research implication:** A location in a later-formed county may have its 1850–1854 records held under the *parent* county. Always confirm the county of origin for a specific year before searching county-level records. The FamilySearch Wiki page for California Genealogy ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)) is the recommended starting point for tracking these splits.

---

## Available Record Types

### 1. Census Records ⭐ *Start Here*

**1852 California State Census** — The single most important census for this era.
- **Coverage:** 1850–1852 | **Access:** 88% name-indexed + images; full-text searchable | FamilySearch volume 006601001 (522 images)
- **Why critical:** The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — several county returns are missing entirely. The 1852 state census is the primary substitute and covers the peak Gold Rush population. This is often the earliest systematic record placing a Gold Rush migrant in a specific California county.

**1850 Federal Census** — First federal enumeration of California.
- **Access:** Indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry; images online — but be aware that some county returns were lost before microfilming. If your county is missing, the 1852 state census is the replacement.

**1860 Federal Census** — Fully intact; captures the settled post-Rush population.
- **Access:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

**Mortality Schedules** — Attached to the 1850 and 1860 censuses; record deaths in the year preceding the census. Useful for tracing individuals who died of mining accidents, disease (cholera, typhoid), and violence.

---

### 2. Mining Claim Records 🔴 *Browse-Only*

- **Record type:** Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco area, 1849–1855 | FamilySearch volume 006601002 (340 images)
- **Access:** **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.** No name search is possible online.
- **Also held at:** County Recorders' offices for each mining county (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, Mariposa, etc.). Physical originals remain at the county level and may not be digitized. Contact individual county recorders for undigitized volumes.
- **Research value:** Documents a miner's presence in a specific district, claim location, partners, and sometimes home state. Can establish an ancestor in California before any census was taken.

---

### 3. Immigration & Arrival Records

**Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858** 🔴 *Browse-Only*
- FamilySearch volume 006601003 (298 images) | **0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse only.**
- Many '49ers arrived by sea — either the full Cape Horn route (5–8 months) or the faster Panama crossing (3–5 weeks by ship + overland). Ship manifests for vessels arriving at **San Francisco** are the primary arrival record.

**Ship Passenger Manifests — San Francisco**
- Held at the **National Archives, Pacific Region (San Bruno, California)** — the major repository for pre-1891 Pacific Coast arrival records. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, *California Genealogy*, [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))
- Also searchable on **Ancestry.com** (U.S. Federal Census Collection and passenger list collections).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including children. Examine the full manifest page — family members traveling together are listed consecutively.

**Overland arrivals** are not captured in port records. Look instead for diaries, journals, and letters at the **Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley)** and **California State Library** — both hold extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections documenting overland migration.

---

### 4. Vital Records (Civil Registration) ⚠️ *Very Sparse for the 1850s*

California had **no statewide civil registration** during the 1850s. Statewide registration did not begin until **1905** (county-level only in this era; the wiki at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records) confirms sparse coverage).

**FamilySearch collections found:**
| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | URL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| California, County Births, 1850–1919 | 1850–1919 | 789,456 | 394,728 | [Collection 2017276](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276) |
| California, County Marriages, 1850–1952 | 1850–1952 | 567,890 | 283,945 | [Collection 1452832](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832) |

> ⚠️ While these collections start in 1850, coverage for the 1850s decade is sparse and uneven. County clerks were newly established and registration was inconsistent. Expect significant gaps — treat a missing vital record as normal for this period, not as proof the event didn't occur.

**Death records:** No county death collection was returned by `collections_search` for the 1845–1865 window specifically. The mortality schedules attached to the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses are the most reliable death documentation for this decade.

**Pre-Rush alternatives:** For Californio/Mexican families predating the Rush, see Mission Records below.

---

### 5. Church Records

**Catholic Mission Records, 1769–1850** (for Spanish/Mexican-era families)
- FamilySearch collection: *California, Mission Records, 1769–1850* | 98,765 records | [Collection 1804372](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372)
- Documents baptisms, marriages, and burials at the 21 Franciscan missions. **Language:** Spanish and Latin. Researcher must be able to read Spanish-language sacramental registers.
- Covers the Californio population preceding the Gold Rush, not the '49er migrants themselves — but essential for tracing families of Mexican or Californio origin present during the Rush.

**Protestant congregations** established rapidly in mining towns (Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian) but records from 1850s mining-camp churches are fragmentary and held locally, if they survive at all. Check denominational archives and the **California State Library**.

**Jewish congregations** in San Francisco (Congregation Sherith Israel, est. 1849; Congregation Emanu-El, est. 1850) kept registers. Contact the congregations directly for 1850s records.

---

### 6. Land Records

- **System:** California is a **federal-land state** — land was distributed via federal patents through the General Land Office.
- **Federal patents:** Search the **Bureau of Land Management (BLM) General Land Office Records** website (glorecords.blm.gov) — free and name-indexed. Many original land grants to Gold Rush settlers are here.
- **County deed books:** Held at the County Recorder's office in each county; not systematically digitized for the 1850s. Physical visit or mail request required for most counties.
- **Mexican-era land grants (Ranchos):** Californio land grants were litigated through the U.S. Land Commission (1851–1856). Records at NARA San Bruno. These are critical for tracing Californio families whose ranchos overlapped the gold fields.

---

### 7. Voter Registration — Great Registers

- FamilySearch collection: *California, Great Registers, 1866–1910* | 1,345,678 records | [Collection 1923340](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340)
- **Note:** This collection begins in **1866** — outside the 1850s target window — but is extremely useful for tracing men who arrived during the Rush and remained. The registers record name, age, physical description, birthplace, occupation, and residence. They function as a de facto directory of adult male residents county by county.
- Covers naturalized citizens and native-born male citizens age 21+. Foreign-born miners who had not naturalized will not appear.

---

### 8. Naturalization Records

- **Pre-1906:** Declarations of intent ("first papers") and petitions for naturalization could be filed in *any court of record* — federal district court, state court, county court. For California in the 1850s, check the U.S. District Court records at **NARA San Bruno** and county superior/district court records.
- Many Gold Rush migrants naturalized quickly to gain voting rights and mining claim eligibility. Naturalization records often state country of birth and sometimes the specific place of origin.
- **Not systematically indexed online for the 1850s.** Physical search at NARA San Bruno or county courthouses required for most.

---

### 9. Military Records

- **California Bear Flag Revolt (1846)** and **Mexican-American War (1846–1848):** Volunteers may have service records at NARA.
- **California Indian Wars / militia records (1850s):** California State Military Museum and the California State Archives hold some militia rosters.
- **Civil War (1861–1865):** California raised Union regiments; service and pension records at NARA (Washington, D.C.) and on **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)).
- **Mexican-American War veterans:** Bounty land warrants (1850 Act) were claimed by veterans of this war — search via NARA or Fold3.

---

### 10. Newspapers

- The **San Francisco Alta California** (est. 1849) and **Sacramento Union** (est. 1851) are the major papers of record; both carried legal notices, ship arrivals, obituaries, and mining district news.
- Dozens of short-lived mining-camp newspapers existed throughout the Mother Lode.
- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) and the **California Digital Newspaper Collection** (cdnc.ucr.edu) both hold digitized 1850s California papers — search obituaries, ship manifests published in papers, and legal notices.
- **Research value:** Ship arrival lists were routinely printed in San Francisco papers — a second documentary layer beyond the official manifests.

---

### 11. Cemetery Records

- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) — the primary online cemetery index; covers major California cemeteries including Gold Rush–era mining sites.
- Many early miners were buried in unmarked or now-lost graves. Cemetery coverage for remote 1850s mining camps is incomplete.
- Physical sexton records (where they survive) are held by local cemetery districts or county archives.

---

### 12. Tax Records

- **State and county assessment rolls** from the early 1850s exist for some counties and can substitute for census years where records are missing. Holdings vary by county — check with the California State Archives and individual county assessor/recorder offices.

---

### 13. Occupational & Organizational Records

- **Fraternal organizations:** Odd Fellows (IOOF) and Masonic lodges were established in California mining towns by the early 1850s. Lodge records (membership, deaths, financial aid) are held at the state grand lodge archives and can document a miner's presence and death.
- **Foreign-language mutual aid societies:** Chinese Six Companies (Huiguan), French benevolent societies, Chilean and Mexican communities maintained records. Holdings are scattered across ethnic community archives.
- **Hospital and institutional records:** Marine Hospital (San Francisco) records for the 1850s are at NARA San Bruno.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections / Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | County Births 1850–1919; County Marriages 1850–1952; Mission Records 1769–1850; Great Registers 1866–1910; California State Census 1850–1852 (88% indexed); Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (browse-only); Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 (browse-only); 14+ digitized volumes total | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1850, 1860); passenger lists; various California collections | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service records; pension files | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery transcriptions statewide | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical California newspapers | Subscription |
| **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| **CDNC** (cdnc.ucr.edu) | Digitized California newspapers, 1846–1922 | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Pacific Region — San Bruno, CA** | Ship passenger manifests (SF port); naturalization records; federal court records; Mexican-era land commission files; Marine Hospital records | In-person; some records reproducible by mail |
| **California State Archives — Sacramento** | State census; county records transferred to state; militia records; legislative records | In-person; some online via Ancestry partnership |
| **California State Library — Sacramento** | Gold Rush manuscript collections; newspapers; county histories | In-person; digitization ongoing |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Gold Rush diaries, journals, letters; Californio manuscripts; overland trail accounts | In-person; appointment required |
| **County Recorders / Courthouses** | Mining claim registers; deed books; probate files; naturalization petitions | In-person or mail; varies by county |
| **BLM California State Office** | Mexican-era rancho land case files | In-person / written request |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following exist but are **not** fully available in any online name-indexed database:
- **Mining claim registers** beyond the FamilySearch browse-only volumes — many county-level volumes remain undigitized
- **County deed books and land transfer records** (most 1850s volumes)
- **1850s naturalization records** (pre-1906 local court filings)
- **County tax assessment rolls** (most counties)
- **Fraternal lodge membership and death records**
- **Foreign-language community organization records** (Chinese, French, Chilean, etc.)
- **Marine Hospital and institutional records at NARA San Bruno**

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1850 federal census — partial destruction:** Several California county returns were lost before microfilming. The **1852 California State Census** (FamilySearch vol. 006601001, 88% indexed) is the primary substitute.
- **1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire:** Destroyed enormous quantities of records stored in San Francisco, including some early county records. San Francisco County vital records before 1906 are largely lost; substitute with church records, newspapers, and the Great Registers.
- **Mining-camp courthouse fires:** Several county seat courthouses burned in the 1850s–1870s. Verify survival before assuming records exist for a specific county.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1852 California State Census** — it is 88% name-indexed on FamilySearch and directly substitutes for destroyed 1850 county returns. It often lists county of residence, which anchors further county-level searching.

2. **Determine the route of arrival** before searching arrival records — sea arrivals (Cape Horn or Panama route) generate San Francisco ship manifests at NARA San Bruno; overland arrivals do not. Overland evidence is in diaries and journals at the Bancroft Library and California State Library.

3. **County boundaries shifted constantly** through the 1850s. If a location is in a county formed after 1850, its earlier records are held under the *parent* county. Confirm the county for each research year before pulling courthouse records.

4. **Mining claim registers are browse-only** on FamilySearch — no name search exists. Know the mining district before browsing (claim registers are organized by district, then chronologically). District can often be established from the census.

5. **The Great Registers (from 1866)** are the best systematic directory of male residents post-Rush. Even though they fall outside the 1850s window, they confirm continued residence and provide birthplace and physical description — valuable for linking a miner to his origin.

6. **Transience is normal** — many '49ers appear in one county in 1852 and a different county in 1860, or left California entirely. If you lose someone between censuses, check neighboring mining counties and consider they may have returned to their home state.

7. **For Chinese, Mexican, Chilean, and French miners**, ethnic-community newspapers, mutual aid society records, and the Foreign Miners' Tax records (held at some county recorders) may be the only surviving documentation, as these groups were often excluded from mainstream civil records.

8. **Newspapers published ship arrival lists** — the *San Francisco Alta California* and *Sacramento Union* both printed passenger names from incoming vessels. The California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) offers free full-text search of digitized issues.

9. **FamilySearch has 14+ digitized volumes** for this period; only 3 were returned in the initial survey. Use FamilySearch's Catalog directly, filtering by California county and date range, to locate additional browse-only volumes not surfaced in this guide.

10. **The Bancroft Library's Gold Rush manuscript collection** is exceptional for this period — diaries, letters, and journals often name traveling companions, mining partners, and associates who may not appear in any official record.

---

# Locality Guide: New York City, Colonial Period (1700s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Founded:** New Amsterdam established by the Dutch West India Company in 1626; seized by England in 1664 and renamed New York. By 1700 it was firmly under British colonial administration as the principal city of the Province of New York.
- **Administrative center:** The city occupied the southern tip of Manhattan (then the entirety of settled New York City). What are today the other four boroughs were separate jurisdictions in the 1700s (Kings County / Brooklyn across the East River; Queens, Richmond, Westchester to the north and east).
- **Parent jurisdiction (colonial):** Province of New York under the British Crown. The provincial capital and governor resided in the city.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic commercial port — trade in furs, grain, lumber, and imported manufactures. Merchant, artisan, and maritime occupations predominated.
- **Ethnic composition:** Notably diverse even by 1700: Dutch families from the original New Amsterdam settlement, English settlers, French Huguenot refugees, Sephardic Jewish merchants, and enslaved Africans who by the mid-1700s constituted roughly 15–20% of the city's population. Germans and Scots arrived throughout the century.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous congregation, records from 1639), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, founded 1697), Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran, Quaker, Shearith Israel synagogue (oldest Jewish congregation in North America, 1654).
- **Key historical events:** 1700s saw rapid population growth; British occupation during the Seven Years' War and the American Revolution (1776–1783, when the city was held by British forces); a major fire in 1776 destroyed a large portion of the city.

## Boundary changes

- The Province of New York (colonial predecessor to New York State, formed 1788) held all provincial records. Probate jurisdiction in the colonial period sat with the **Prerogative Court of New York** — a single provincial body, not a county court — meaning wills and administrations for the entire province, including the city, were proved there.
- Manhattan (New York County) was the only settled borough in the modern sense during the 1700s. Brooklyn/Kings County, Queens County, Richmond County (Staten Island), and the Bronx areas were separate rural jurisdictions with their own record sets.
- New York became a U.S. state in 1788; civil infrastructure for record-keeping changed after that date. Research in the 1700s falls almost entirely within colonial/provincial record systems.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** **No civil registration existed in New York during the 1700s.** Statewide civil registration of marriages did not begin until 1880; births and deaths likewise began in the 1880s at the state level. NYC itself began local registration somewhat earlier (city-level death registration ca. 1853), but this is entirely outside the colonial period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the **only** source for baptisms, marriages, and burials in the 1700s. See Church Records below.

### Church records ⭐ *Primary source for the 1700s*

- **FamilySearch collection:** *New York, Church Records, 1640–1940* (Collection ID 1469062) — 2,345,678 indexed records, 1,172,839 images. **Access: Indexed + images** at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062). Free.
- **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, NYC, 1700–1776:** One digitized image volume found in FamilySearch's digitized holdings (Image Group 007733180, 211 images). ⚠️ **Browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, and recorded in Dutch.** You must read each page image directly; knowledge of 18th-century Dutch is required. Earliest continuous series; begins 1639.
- **Trinity Church (Anglican/Episcopal):** Founded 1697. Extensive baptism, marriage, and burial registers for the 1700s. Published and indexed in the *New-York Genealogical and Biographical Record*; also held at the Trinity Church Archives, New York City.
- **Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran, Quaker, Shearith Israel (Jewish):** Records exist and some are published or microfilmed. Holdings vary — check the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) and the New-York Historical Society (N-YHS).
- **Language note:** Dutch Reformed registers through at least the 1730s–1740s were kept in Dutch. Anglican and Presbyterian registers are in English.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census was **1790**, so this falls just outside the 1700s target. The 1790 census (indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry) is the earliest federal source, covering households at the very end of the era.
- **Colonial enumerations:** The Province of New York conducted several population counts and tax-based enumerations in the 1700s. The wiki sources note tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards. These are not the same as a modern census but can establish presence and taxable wealth.
- **No federal census coverage for 1700–1789.** Tax lists and church membership lists are the functional substitutes.

### Probate records

- **FamilySearch collection:** *New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971* (Collection ID 1542780) — 987,654 indexed records, 493,827 images. **Access: Indexed + images** at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780). Free.
- **Colonial-era probate jurisdiction:** The **Prerogative Court of New York** handled all probate for the Province — not a county surrogate court. Wills proved before this court are indexed and abstracted in the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the New-York Historical Society (source: wiki_search result, [familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)). This is a key finding aid.
- **What to expect:** Wills, administrations, inventories. Probate records frequently name wives, children, and other relatives and are often the best evidence of family relationships when no church or vital record survives.

### Land records

- **FamilySearch collection:** *New York, Land Records, 1630–1975* (Collection ID 2078654) — 1,567,890 indexed records, 783,945 images. **Access: Indexed + images** at [familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654). Free.
- **System:** Colonial New York used a Dutch-influenced metes-and-bounds system supplemented by English royal patents and grants. Land patents for large tracts were issued by the colonial governor.
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** The New York State Archives holds the colonial land records and patent series (source: wiki_search result). Many have been microfilmed.

### Tax records

- **FamilySearch collection:** *New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804* (Collection ID 1678432) — 123,456 indexed records, 61,728 images. **Access: Indexed + images** at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432). This collection begins at the very end of the target period and into the early republic — useful for families continuing past 1800.
- **Colonial tax lists:** Ward-level tax assessment lists survive for some years during the colonial period and are noted in the wiki_search results. These are held at the New York State Archives and the N-YHS; digitization status for the pre-1799 years is not confirmed by any FamilySearch volume or collection result.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the best substitute for census years in the 1700–1789 period.

### Military records

- **Colonial militia rolls:** The wiki notes that colonial New York Province maintained militia rolls listing men of military age — useful for identifying male residents. Source: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), French and Indian War / Seven Years' War (1754–1763), American Revolutionary War (1775–1783 — NYC was British-held 1776–1783).
- **Fold3:** Curated military records resource returned by the external links search ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)), subscription-based. Holds colonial, Revolutionary War, and early national military records.
- **NARA (National Archives):** [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) — holds Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants.

### Court records

- **Mayor's Court of New York City:** The primary civil and criminal court of the city in the colonial era. Minute books and case files survive and are held at the New York City Municipal Archives and the New York State Archives. Source: wiki_search result.
- **Court of Chancery and Supreme Court of Judicature** operated at the provincial level.
- **Naturalizations:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record. Colonial-era denizations and naturalizations were granted by the provincial government.

### Cemetery records

- **FindAGrave:** [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com) returned as a curated external resource. Many colonial-era NYC burials (Trinity Churchyard, Dutch Reformed burial grounds) are transcribed here.
- **Trinity Churchyard** (Lower Manhattan) is one of the oldest surviving burial grounds in the US, with burials through the entire 1700s.
- **Physical sexton records** for some churches survive at the NYGBS and N-YHS.

### Newspaper records

- **New York Gazette (founded 1725):** The first newspaper published in New York; ran through the colonial period. Contains legal notices, ship arrivals, runaway advertisements (critical for researching enslaved persons), and some vital notices. Source: Wikipedia.
- **Newspapers.com:** [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) returned as a curated external resource (subscription). Coverage for 18th-century NYC papers varies.
- **Content value:** Colonial newspapers are indispensable for free Black and enslaved individuals, merchants, mariners, and anyone involved in legal disputes.

### Immigration and shipping records

- **NYC was the primary Atlantic port** for arrivals to the northeastern colonies in the 1700s. Passenger lists and ship manifests from the colonial period are fragmentary compared to later periods.
- **NARA:** [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) holds early passenger arrival records and naturalization files.
- **Published ship lists** for Dutch-period (pre-1664) arrivals have been compiled; British-period arrivals are less systematically recorded before 1820.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1640–1940 (2.3M records); Land Records 1630–1975 (1.6M); Probate Records 1629–1971 (987K); Tax Assessment Rolls 1799–1804 (123K) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (starts 1790); colonial-era NY materials | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Colonial militia, Revolutionary War service records, pension files | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including colonial NYC | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions including Trinity Churchyard | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, early naturalization, passenger lists | Free / in-person |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts, Mayor's Court records, provincial land patents, tax lists | In-person; some microfilmed |
| New York City Municipal Archives | City-level court records, early deeds, vital records (post-1853) | In-person; some online |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Published abstracts, church records, surname files | In-person (NYC); some online via Ancestry |
| New-York Historical Society (N-YHS) | *Abstracts of Wills* series, colonial manuscripts, church registers | In-person (NYC); published volumes widely available |
| Trinity Church Archives (NYC) | Anglican/Episcopal baptism, marriage, and burial registers from 1697 | By appointment |
| Dutch Reformed Church Archives | Reformed church baptism and marriage registers | Contact Collegiate Church of New York City |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types are confirmed or likely to exist only in physical form for the 1700s NYC target period:

- **Pre-1799 ward-level tax lists** — no FamilySearch volume or indexed collection found covering these years
- **Mayor's Court minute books and case files** — held at NYC Municipal Archives and NY State Archives; not confirmed digitized/indexed
- **Colonial militia rolls** — physical/microfilm; not found in FamilySearch collections or volumes for this period
- **Dutch Reformed church volumes prior to the one digitized volume (007733180)** — additional volumes may exist at the Collegiate Church Archives in forms not indexed on FamilySearch
- **Huguenot, Lutheran, and Quaker registers** — partially published; originals at denominational archives

---

## Known record losses

- The **Great Fire of 1776** destroyed roughly a quarter of lower Manhattan during the British occupation of New York. Some church and civic records held in those buildings were lost.
- **Dutch-period records (pre-1664)** are sparse; many were transferred to the Netherlands or lost.
- **No civil vital registration** existed for the entire 1700s — there are no birth, marriage, or death certificates. Church registers, probate, and newspaper notices are the only contemporaneous sources for vital events.

---

## Research tips

1. **Church records first.** With no civil registration, the baptism, marriage, and burial registers of whichever denomination your family belonged to are the core source. Identify the family's denomination before searching.
2. **Dutch Reformed registers require Dutch.** The one digitized volume (Image Group 007733180, 1700–1776, 211 images) is browse-only and in Dutch — you cannot name-search it. Either read Dutch or use a translation resource.
3. **The *Abstracts of Wills* is an essential finding aid** for the Prerogative Court of New York. Published by the New-York Historical Society, it indexes colonial-era probate across the entire province. Search it before trying to locate original wills.
4. **Search the FamilySearch Church Records collection (1469062) first** for indexed church entries; then check whether the underlying volume for your denomination is browse-only.
5. **Tax lists substitute for the missing census.** The 1700s predate the 1790 federal census; ward-level tax lists are the best way to establish that an ancestor was present in a given year.
6. **Manhattan ≠ all of colonial NYC.** Kings (Brooklyn), Queens, and Richmond Counties were separate jurisdictions with their own church, probate, and land records. If your family was in an outer area, search those county record sets as well.
7. **The NYGBS is the specialist society for this research.** Their *New York Genealogical and Biographical Record* (published since 1870) has abstracted and published many colonial-era NYC records not yet digitized elsewhere.
8. **Enslaved persons:** colonial NYC had a substantial enslaved population. Records appear in slave owner probate inventories, church baptism registers (some churches baptized enslaved persons), newspaper runaway advertisements, and manumission records. The NY Manumission Society records (post-1785) are at the N-YHS.
9. **Post-1790 continuity:** The 1790 federal census (indexed, free on FamilySearch) immediately follows the colonial period and captures the same families — always search it for context on 1700s households.
10. **The New York Colonial Manuscripts** at the New York State Archives are the authoritative source for provincial government records — land patents, council minutes, and correspondence — and are essential for propertied families.

# Locality Research Guide
## Virginia — American Revolutionary War Era (1775–1783)
### Focus: Military Service & Wartime Activities

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies and adopted its state constitution in **June 1776**, shifting from colonial to state governance mid-war. County-level record-keeping dates from the **1630s**, making Virginia one of the best-documented pre-federal jurisdictions in America. The county courthouse — not a central state registry — was the hub of legal, land, and vital life-event documentation throughout this period.

**Critical gap:** The 1790 federal census for Virginia was **destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814**. The **1782–1783 personal property tax lists** are the accepted substitute and serve as the closest enumeration to the war years. Plan your research around these rather than a census.

Virginia had **no statewide civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths during 1775–1783 — that didn't begin until **1853**. Church records (chiefly Anglican/Episcopal vestry books and parish registers) are the primary source for vital events in this period.

---

## Record Categories

### ⚔️ 1. Military Service Records
**The first stop for any Revolutionary War ancestor.**

| Source | Record Type | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| NARA Record Group 93 | Continental Line service records, muster rolls | National Archives, Washington D.C. | Microfilm / Fold3.com (many digitized & indexed) |
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records | Library of Virginia | Physical and partial online finding aids |
| Library of Virginia | Virginia State Navy records (published) | Library of Virginia | Published volumes; some digitized |
| FamilySearch collection [1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) | Virginia Military Records, 1775–1783 | FamilySearch.org | **Indexed + images online** |

> **What to look for:** Unit rosters identify regiment and company; muster rolls show dates of service, pay, and sometimes physical descriptions. The 16 Virginia Continental Line regiments each have separate muster rolls — know your ancestor's regiment if possible. State militia service was separate from Continental service and is documented primarily at the Library of Virginia.
>
> *Source: [Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*

---

### 🏅 2. Pension & Bounty Land Warrant Files
**Often the richest biographical sources for veterans and their families.**

| Source | Record Type | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| NARA Record Group 15 | Pension & bounty-land warrant application files | National Archives | Microfilm; many on Fold3.com (indexed) |
| Virginia State Library / Library of Virginia | Bounty land warrant & survey records (Virginia Military District of Ohio) | Library of Virginia | Physical; partial finding aids online |

> Pension applications frequently include **sworn depositions** from the veteran or widow, naming children, neighbors, and fellow soldiers. They are genealogically invaluable — treat them as high-priority sources. Virginia veterans who qualified received bounty lands in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** (not Virginia proper); warrant and survey records connecting a veteran to that grant are at the Library of Virginia.
>
> **Fold3.com** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) hosts digitized and indexed pension files — check there before requesting microfilm from NARA.
>
> *Source: [Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)*

---

### 📋 3. Tax Records (Substitute Census for 1775–1783)
**Essential — replace the destroyed 1790 census.**

| FamilySearch Collection | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) (id: 1456723) | 1782–1850 | Images available on FamilySearch |

> The **1782 and 1783 personal property tax lists** are the earliest post-war enumeration. They list free white males (and sometimes enslaved persons separately), taxable property, and horses — enough to locate a family in a specific county. Because the 1790 census is gone for Virginia, these lists are the only way to place families geographically near the end of the war.

---

### ⛪ 4. Church Records (Vital Events — Births, Marriages, Burials)
**Primary source for vital events; no civil registration existed.**

| FamilySearch Collection | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230) (id: 1598230) | 1680–1929 | Images available on FamilySearch |

> The **Church of England (Anglican)**, which became the **Protestant Episcopal Church** after independence, was the established church of colonial Virginia. Vestry books and parish registers are the closest equivalent to vital records for 1775–1783. Many survive at the **Library of Virginia** and the **Virginia Historical Society** (now the Virginia Museum of History & Culture).
>
> **Dissenters** — Baptists, Presbyterians, Quakers, Methodists — were a growing force during the Revolution; their records are held by denominational archives and local meetings/congregations, not centrally. Quaker meeting records (many microfilmed by FamilySearch) are especially well-preserved and can document pacifist families who refused military service.

---

### 🏡 5. Land, Marriage & Will Records
**Track family property, relationships, and estates across the war years.**

| FamilySearch Collection | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) (id: 1734285) | 1600–1900 | Images available on FamilySearch |

> Land deeds recorded at the **county courthouse** document sales, gifts, and mortgages that can establish family relationships and economic status during wartime. Marriage bonds (filed with the county clerk) predate formal marriage registers. Wills and estate inventories from this period sometimes reference military service, debts owed by the estate, or property confiscated during the war.
>
> **Loyalist/confiscated property:** Virginia passed confiscation acts during the Revolution. Records of sequestered Loyalist estates are held at the Library of Virginia and can document families on both sides of the conflict.

---

### 🏛️ 6. County Court Records
**The backbone of Virginia genealogy — civil, criminal, and administrative.**

| FamilySearch Collection | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567) (id: 2134567) | 1650–1920 | Images available on FamilySearch |

> County order books record nearly every legal transaction: orphan apprenticeships (naming fathers who died), guardianship bonds, debt suits, road orders, and appointments of overseers of the poor. During the Revolution these books also contain **militia musters, impressment orders, and supply requisitions** — documenting wartime community activities beyond individual service.

---

### 📰 7. Newspapers & Published Sources
**Contemporary reporting on the war, deaths, and social life.**

| Repository | Resource | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers, including Virginia Gazette | [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) (subscription) |
| Library of Virginia | *Virginia Soldiers of the American Revolution* (published volumes) | Physical; some digitized |
| DAR / SAR | Published lineage and membership files | DAR Library, Washington D.C.; online indexes |

> The **Virginia Gazette** (published in Williamsburg) reported military appointments, deaths of officers, and political events during the war. Virginia also has extensive **published abstracts** of pension files and militia rosters — check volumes compiled by researchers like John Frederick Dorman and Bockstruck's *Virginia's Colonial Soldiers*.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Location | What's There |
|---|---|---|

> ⚠️ **Verify collection record counts and indexing percentages directly at FamilySearch.org** before assuming name-searchability — some collections may be browse-only images requiring page-by-page examination.

---

## Researcher's Quirks & Gotchas

1. **The 1790 Virginia census is gone.** Always use the 1782–1783 personal property tax lists as your stand-in enumeration for locating families at war's end.
2. **No statewide vital registration until 1853.** For births, marriages, and deaths in 1775–1783, go to Anglican vestry books and parish registers first, then dissenting church records.
3. **Continental service ≠ militia service.** A man could serve in both — and pension records often describe both. NARA holds Continental records; the Library of Virginia holds militia records. Search both.
4. **Virginia Military District bounty lands are in Ohio, not Virginia.** If your veteran received a land bounty, the warrant and survey will be at the Library of Virginia, but the land itself was in Ohio.
5. **Loyalist families are under-researched.** Virginia confiscation acts created a paper trail — property sequestration records at the Library of Virginia can document families who remained Crown sympathizers.
6. **County boundaries shifted frequently.** New counties were carved from parent counties throughout this era. Identify which county your ancestor's locality belonged to *in 1775–1783* — records filed before a county split remain in the parent county's books.
7. **Fold3 and Ancestry complement FamilySearch.** NARA's pension files are split between Fold3 (many digitized) and physical microfilm. Cross-check all three platforms before concluding a file doesn't exist.

---

## Suggested Search Order

1. **FamilySearch** — *Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783* (collection 1945678) for a quick name search
2. **Fold3.com** — Revolutionary War pension & bounty land files (NARA RG 15), compiled service records (RG 93)
3. **FamilySearch** — *Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850* to place the family geographically
4. **FamilySearch** — *Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929* for vital events
5. **FamilySearch** — *Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records* and *County Court Records* for family context
6. **Library of Virginia** (in person or online catalog) for militia records, state navy records, and manuscript collections not yet digitized

---

*Wiki references: [Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War) · [Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands) · Wikipedia: [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)*

---

A few things worth highlighting as you plan your research:

- **Pension files are your richest source.** If your ancestor served long enough to qualify, the NARA RG 15 pension application will often name his wife, children, neighbors who testified, and sometimes give a detailed account of his service. Widows' pensions (filed years later) can be even more detailed.
- **Don't overlook women and non-combatants.** County court records, vestry books, and property records document families who stayed home — wives managing estates, widows petitioning for support, and civilian suppliers who appear in wartime impressment records.
- **The Library of Virginia is irreplaceable.** Much of what distinguishes Virginia Revolutionary War research from other states lives there in manuscript form — not yet digitized, not on FamilySearch. A visit or a request through their online catalog and reference service is often necessary for deep militia and state-level records.

# 📍 Locality Research Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana — Early 1800s (c. 1800–1850)

## Jurisdictional Context

New Orleans was founded in **1718** by France, transferred to **Spain in 1763**, retroceded briefly to France in 1800, then sold to the United States in the **Louisiana Purchase of 1803**. It was part of the **Territory of Orleans (1804–1812)** before Louisiana achieved statehood as the **18th state in 1812**. New Orleans sits in **Orleans Parish** — and Louisiana uses *parishes*, not counties, its entire civil law tradition flowing from the Napoleonic Code rather than English common law. This distinction pervades every record type: legal documents follow civil law forms, and notarial records are central to documentation in ways unlike anywhere else in the United States.

This means your target period, the early 1800s, spans **three overlapping records regimes**: (1) the tail end of Spanish colonial administration, (2) the US territorial period, and (3) early Louisiana statehood. Records created under each regime are held in different repositories and written in different languages (Spanish, French, and English).

---

## ⚠️ The Disaster Landscape

New Orleans suffered a sequence of catastrophic record losses. Understanding what was lost — and what survived — is the foundation of any research strategy here.

| Event | Year | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| **Great New Orleans Fire** | 1788 | Destroyed ~856 of 1,100 structures in the French Quarter; many Spanish colonial-era civic records burned |
| **Second Great Fire** | 1794 | Destroyed another ~200 buildings; further losses to administrative and church records |
| **Yellow fever epidemics** | Endemic throughout period (worst peaks 1820s–1850s) | Generated massive mortality; disrupted recordkeeping institutions |
| **Hurricanes and flooding** | Recurring | Ongoing damage to paper archives throughout the 19th century |

*(Sources: Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans; FamilySearch Wiki chunk — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)*

---

## What Survived — and Where to Find It

### 1. 📖 Sacramental / Church Records (BEST SURVIVING SOURCE)

**What survived:** The sacramental registers of **St. Louis Cathedral** — baptisms, marriages, and burials — date from **1731** and survived the fires, though with gaps. Because Louisiana's civil registration of vital events did not begin at the statewide level until **1918** (city of New Orleans began earlier, around 1790s under Spanish administration, but coverage was inconsistent), church records are effectively the *only* vital record source for most of the early 1800s.

**FamilySearch collection:** **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** (collection ID 1612905) — covers the target period and includes Catholic registers from New Orleans parishes. Available at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905

**Repository:** The **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** holds the originals. Many registers have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. The **Archdiocese of New Orleans** also published a multi-volume index to early sacramental records.

**Language warning:** Records from the Spanish and early American periods are in **Spanish and/or French**. Researchers must be able to read the original language or obtain a translation.

---

### 2. 📜 Notarial Records (EXCEPTIONAL SURVIVAL — HIGHEST RESEARCH VALUE)

**What survived:** This is the single most remarkable survival story for New Orleans. Because Louisiana's civil law system required virtually every significant legal transaction — sales, contracts, wills, manumissions, marriage contracts, mortgages, slave sales — to be executed before a notary, notarial records are extraordinarily rich. The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over **30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734**, making it one of the largest repositories of its kind in the Western Hemisphere. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)*

**FamilySearch digitized volume:** Volume **004990115** — *Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies), 1803–1820*, Orleans Parish. **167 images. 0% name-indexed. Not full-text searchable.** This volume must be browsed **image by image** with no name search. Records are in **French and English**. This is the direct digital evidence of records that survived the earlier fires in microfilm copy form.

**Repository:** **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**, 1340 Poydras Street, New Orleans. Physical access required for the bulk of holdings beyond what FamilySearch has digitized.

**Why this matters as a substitute:** When church, civil, or court records are missing, notarial records frequently contain the same facts embedded in contracts — a sale of property might name a deceased parent, a marriage contract names both families, a succession (will/probate) names all heirs. Search notarial records whenever other record types have gaps.

---

### 3. ⚖️ Probate / Succession Records

**What survived:** Louisiana calls probate **"successions."** Because succession proceedings were handled through the civil courts and notarial system, substantial records survive even for the early 1800s.

**FamilySearch collection:** **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** (collection ID 2078341) — covers the full target period. Available at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341

*(Source: collections_search result for Louisiana)*

**Repository:** Territorial and early statehood succession records are held at the **Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge**, as well as at the **Orleans Parish Civil District Court** and the **Louisiana Historical Center** in New Orleans.

---

### 4. 💀 Death / Mortality Records

**FamilySearch collection:** **Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964** (collection ID 1543892) — begins in **1819**, so it covers the later portion of the early 1800s. Available at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892

For deaths before 1819, researchers must rely on church burial registers (see #1 above), notarial succession records (#3), and newspaper death notices.

---

### 5. 💒 Marriage Records

**FamilySearch collection:** **Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957** (collection ID 1798054) — begins **1837**, so it covers only the later part of this period. For marriages before 1837, the primary source is church sacramental registers and notarial marriage contracts.

Available at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054

---

### 6. 🏛️ Spanish Colonial / Cabildo Records

**What survived:** The **Cabildo** was the Spanish colonial governing body (1769–1803). Some of its administrative records survived the fires and are held at the **Louisiana State Archives** and the **Louisiana Historical Center** (a division of the Louisiana State Museum). *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki chunk — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)*

**Critical substitute — Spain's archives:** Many colonial records were duplicated and sent to Spain. The **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)** in Seville and the **Archivo General de Simancas** hold copies that survived the 1788 and 1794 fires precisely because they were never in New Orleans. This is an essential lookup for any ancestor present before 1803. The AGI has begun digitizing portions of its holdings at **pares.mcu.es**.

---

### 7. 🇫🇷 French Colonial Records (Pre-1763 Background / Duplicate Source)

For families with roots stretching into the French colonial era, the **Archives nationales d'outre-mer (ANOM)** in Aix-en-Provence, France holds French colonial records, some of which relate to Louisiana. These serve as a substitute source when no New Orleans-held original survives.

---

### 8. 🇺🇸 Federal Records (Post-1803)

After the Louisiana Purchase, US federal records begin:

| Record | Years | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **US Federal Census** | 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 | Orleans Parish included. Slave schedules in 1850. |
| **Territorial/Federal Land Patents** | 1803 onward | BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal land grants confirming land titles |
| **Military Records — War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans** | 1812–1815 | Service records and pension files at NARA; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| **Passenger Lists** | 1800–1850 | New Orleans was the largest US port of entry after New York. NARA holds passenger arrival lists; Ancestry.com and FamilySearch have digitized sets |

---

### 9. 📰 Newspapers as Substitute Sources

New Orleans newspapers from the early 1800s (*Louisiana Gazette*, founded 1804; *L'Ami des Lois*; *New Orleans Bee / L'Abeille*) regularly published birth, marriage, and death notices. These function as a vital record substitute when civil or church records are missing.

**Access:** **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) and the **Library of Congress Chronicling America** project (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) have digitized early Louisiana newspapers.

---

### 10. 🪦 Cemetery Records

New Orleans's famous above-ground tomb cemeteries hold significant burial evidence. **St. Louis Cemetery No. 1** (founded 1789) and **St. Louis Cemetery No. 2** (founded 1823) are the primary ones for the target period.

**Access:** **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial New Orleans cemetery transcriptions. The **Save Our Cemeteries** organization also maintains databases.

---

### 11. 🔍 Additional Unique Louisiana Record Types

Because of the civil law system, Louisiana generated record types not found elsewhere in the US:

- **Tutorships** — guardianship of minors; filed in district court, name parents and children
- **Interdictions** — legal incompetency proceedings; name family members
- **Emancipation records** — both for enslaved persons and for those emancipating them; in notarial records
- **Free People of Color records** — New Orleans had a large, legally distinct *gens de couleur libres* community whose records are found in church registers, notarial acts, and Spanish colonial archives

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)*

---
