| Church Records, 1718–1925 (FS coll. 1612905) | **Indexed + images** | Best online access for Catholic vital events |
| Probate/Succession Records, 1756–1984 (FS coll. 2078341) | **Indexed + images** | Covers full target period |
| Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (FS coll. 1798054) | **Indexed + images** | Starts 1837 only |
| Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (FS coll. 1543892) | **Index only** (0 images) | Starts 1819 |
| Notarial Acts 1803–1820 (FS vol. 004990115) | **Browse-only images** | 167 images, 0% indexed, French/English; must be browsed page by page |
| Spanish colonial / Cabildo records | **Physical / microfilm** | Louisiana State Archives and Louisiana Historical Center |
| Spanish duplicate records | **Physical (Spain)** | AGI Seville (pares.mcu.es has partial digitization) |
| French colonial records | **Physical (France)** | ANOM, Aix-en-Provence |

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | 30M+ pages of notarial acts, 1734–present | On-site; some microfilm via FamilySearch |
| **Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge** | Territorial/statehood records, successions | On-site and some online |
| **Louisiana Historical Center (State Museum), New Orleans** | Cabildo records, colonial-era documents | On-site |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | St. Louis Cathedral and parish registers | On-site and some microfilm |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal census, military, passenger lists | NARA; Ancestry; Fold3 |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville (Spain)** | Duplicate Spanish colonial records | pares.mcu.es (partial digitization) |
| **ANOM, Aix-en-Provence (France)** | French colonial records | On-site; partial digitization |

---

## Researcher Quirks and Warnings

1. **Search for the Spanish duplicate first for anything pre-1803.** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed originals; Spain's AGI in Seville holds copies of colonial records that never burned. This is the single most important substitute strategy for the colonial/early period.

2. **Notarial records are the backbone — not a last resort.** Unlike other states where you reach for notarial/court records only after vital records fail, in New Orleans you should search notarial records *first* or in parallel. They contain embedded vital facts (birth, death, family relationships) for nearly every free person of means.

3. **Civil registration of births/marriages/deaths did not begin statewide until 1918.** For the entire early 1800s, church registers and notarial records are the de facto civil registration system. "No civil registration" is not a dead end — it's a redirect.

4. **Record language shifts by era.** Spanish colonial records are in Spanish; French colonial and early American-era records are often in French; post-1803 records increasingly shift to English but French remained common in New Orleans through the 1840s. Plan for translation needs.

5. **Orleans Parish is the city.** Unlike most Louisiana parishes, Orleans Parish is coterminous with the city of New Orleans — no rural township confusion.

6. **Free People of Color form a distinct research community.** New Orleans had one of the largest free Black populations in antebellum America. Their records appear in Catholic sacramental registers (which recorded baptisms and marriages across racial lines, with notations), Spanish colonial free-person registers, notarial acts, and eventually census free schedules.

7. **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana and New Orleans returned only generic content in this session.** For the most current, locality-specific guidance, visit directly: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy.

---

> **Bottom line:** New Orleans in the early 1800s is a challenging but rewarding research environment. The fires of 1788 and 1794 are real obstacles, but two institutions preserved a remarkable amount: the Catholic Church (whose sacramental registers date from 1731) and the notarial system (30+ million pages surviving at the Notarial Archives). When local records fail, look to Spain's Archivo General de Indias for Spanish-era duplicates, and to federal records (census, land, military, passenger lists) for the post-1803 period. The unique civil law record types — successions, tutorships, notarial contracts — are often richer than their common-law equivalents and deserve priority attention.

# Locality Research Guide: Boston Port of Entry, 1840s
**Place:** Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts, United States
**Period:** 1820–1870 (centred on the 1840s)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Boston sits in Suffolk County and has been part of Massachusetts since statehood (1788). In the 1840s it was one of the five major U.S. ports of entry. The Great Famine (1845–1852) drove a massive surge of Irish arrivals; by 1850 more than a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born. Immigrants settled first in the North End and Fort Hill neighbourhoods. Records relevant to these arrivals fall across federal, state, town, and church jurisdictions — each level captures different information.

> **Key limitation of 1840s arrivals lists:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Massachusetts Immigration — Port of Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)), customs passenger lists of this era capture only **name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin** — not hometown, last residence, or next of kin. The richer detail found in post-1890 Ellis Island manifests does not exist here.

---

## Record Survey

### 1. 🚢 Customs Passenger Lists — **Prime Source**

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection** | [Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) (Collection ID 1784312) |
| **Date range** | 1820–1891 — fully covers the 1840s |
| **Digitization** | **Indexed + images** (1,234,567 indexed records; 617,283 images) |
| **Originals** | National Archives Record Group 36; held at the **National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA** |
| **Also online** | [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/) |

In addition, the volume search returned a specific image group directly for this period:

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch volume** | Image Group **003345210** — *Passenger Lists, Port of Boston, 1840–1850* |
| **Images** | 389 pages |
| **Digitization** | ⚠️ **Full-text searchable, NOT name-indexed** (recordSearchablePercent: 3%) — use FamilySearch full-text search, not name search; the volume cannot be browsed by surname alone |
| **Language** | English |

---

### 2. 📋 Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths in Boston after Arrival)

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection** | [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) (Collection ID 2061550) |
| **Date range** | 1620–1890 |
| **Digitization** | **Indexed + images** (3,456,789 indexed records; 1,728,394 images) |

Massachusetts has an exceptionally deep tradition of town-level vital registration — town clerks were recording births, marriages, and deaths long before the statehood era. Immigrants who settled in Boston and had children, married, or died there from the 1840s onward will appear in Boston's own town vital registers within this collection. Note that the **town** series is the primary layer for this period; the collection itself dates from 1620.

---

### 3. ⛪ Church Records

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection** | [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) (Collection ID 1921657) |
| **Date range** | 1630–1920 |
| **Digitization** | **Indexed + images** (987,654 indexed records; 493,827 images) |
| **Key parishes for Irish immigrants** | Cathedral of the Holy Cross; St. Patrick's (per [Massachusetts Church Records — Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)) |
| **Original registers** | **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** — not fully digitized on FamilySearch; contact the Archdiocese directly for 1840s Catholic registers |

⚠️ Church records are **essential** for Irish Catholic immigrants in this period because baptism, marriage, and burial registers were often recorded more carefully at the parish than in civil records. If a family cannot be found in town vital records, the parish register is the next step.

---

### 4. 📜 Naturalization Records

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection** | [Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) (Collection ID 1459213) |
| **Date range** | 1790–1906 |
| **Digitization** | **Indexed + images** (345,678 indexed records; 172,839 images) |

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — federal, state, or local. For 1840s Boston arrivals, check both **Suffolk County courts** and the **U.S. District Court for Massachusetts** (records at NARA Waltham). First papers (declaration of intent) and second papers (petition/oath) are separate filings and may be years apart; both can contain place of birth and arrival information.

---

### 5. 👥 Federal Census Records

| | |
|---|---|
| **Repository** | [Ancestry.com — U.S. Federal Census Collection](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| **Key enumerations** | 1850 (first census to list every household member by name with birthplace by country) and 1860 |

The 1850 census is often the first place to confirm an immigrant's country of origin and household composition after the 1840s arrival wave. Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year before each census and may document immigrants who died shortly after arrival.

---

### 6. ⚖️ Probate Records

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection** | [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) (Collection ID 1678901) |
| **Date range** | 1635–1991 |
| **Digitization** | **Indexed + images** (567,890 indexed records; 283,945 images) |

Wills and estate inventories can identify family members, places of origin, and property — useful for confirming kinship and settlement patterns after arrival.

---

### 7. 📰 Newspapers — *The Pilot* Missing-Persons Database

The Wikipedia result for Boston specifically notes that *The Pilot* (Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper) **published arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements** for Irish immigrants throughout the 1840s and beyond. This is a critical supplement when passenger lists fail:

- Available via the **Boston Public Library** and digitized collections at [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)
- Searchable separately through the *[Boston Pilot Missing Persons Database](http://www.infowanted.bc.edu/)* (a dedicated project transcribing these ads)

---

### 8. ⚔️ Military Records

| | |
|---|---|
| **Repository** | [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) — service records, pension files, bounty land warrants |
| **Also at** | [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/) — originals for service and pension records |

Relevant if an immigrant ancestor served in the Mexican-American War (1846–1848) or later the Civil War after settling in Boston.

---

### 9. 🪦 Cemetery Records

| | |
|---|---|
| **Repository** | [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) |

Transcriptions and photographs of grave markers can confirm death dates, ages, and family groupings among 1840s settler communities.

---

## Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Indexed passenger lists, town vital records, church records, naturalization records, probate records (all collections above) |
| **National Archives at Boston — Waltham, MA** | Original customs passenger lists (RG 36), federal court naturalization records, federal census originals |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Original Catholic parish registers (Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and other Boston parishes) not fully digitized |
| **Boston Public Library** | Historical newspapers including *The Pilot*; city directories; local history collections |
| **Massachusetts State Archives** | State-level vital records, some naturalization records, state censuses (1855, 1865) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census collection; duplicate passenger list indexes |
| **Newspapers.com / Fold3 / Find A Grave** | Historical newspapers, military records, cemetery transcriptions |

---

## Research Quirks to Know

1. **1840s passenger lists are thin records.** Expect only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — the detail of later manifests is absent. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston))

2. **Volume 003345210 is full-text searchable but only 3% name-indexed.** Run a full-text search rather than a name search when using this volume on FamilySearch.

3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered.** There is no single index — check Suffolk County Superior Court, the U.S. District Court (NARA Waltham), and municipal court records.

4. **Catholic parish registers at the Archdiocese of Boston Archives are not fully on FamilySearch.** For 1840s Irish Catholic immigrants, the FamilySearch church records collection is a starting point, but you may need to contact the Archdiocese directly.

5. **Use *The Pilot* missing-persons ads as a passenger-list substitute.** Many Irish arrivals who cannot be found in customs lists placed or were named in ads in *The Pilot*. ([Source: Wikipedia — Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston))

6. **FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts-specific pages** did not load in this session. For additional research strategies, consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy directly.

---

**Bottom line:** Start with the FamilySearch [Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) (name-indexed) and supplement with a full-text search of Image Group 003345210. Follow arrivals forward into the 1850/1860 census, town vital records, and Catholic parish registers. If the passenger list fails, *The Pilot* missing-persons database is the best fallback for Irish immigrants specifically. Naturalization papers are the best source for birthplace detail beyond what the 1840s customs list provides.

---

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory (Present-Day Oklahoma), 1830–1880

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Designation:** Indian Territory was a federally administered region — not a U.S. state or organized territory with standard county government — set aside under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 for the forced relocation of Native American tribes, primarily from the southeastern United States.
- **Administrative center:** No single capital; each tribal nation maintained its own government (e.g., Tahlequah for the Cherokee, Tishomingo for the Chickasaw).
- **Major tribal nations present:** The Five Civilized Tribes — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — were the largest groups relocated via the Trail of Tears from the 1830s onward.
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the tools for this jurisdiction.
- **Government structure:** Tribal self-governance under federal oversight through the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA). There was no U.S. territorial civil government during this period — record-keeping authority rested with tribal nations and federal agencies.
- **Oklahoma statehood:** 1907. Records created before statehood fall under Indian Territory or tribal jurisdiction, not Oklahoma state records.

---

## Boundary and Jurisdictional Notes

- Indian Territory had no standard U.S. county boundaries during the mid-1800s. Land was organized by tribal nation rather than by county.
- After 1890, Oklahoma Territory was carved out of the western portion of Indian Territory; from 1890 to 1907, the two territories existed side by side. Records from the eastern portion (the Five Tribes' homeland) remain under Indian Territory provenance; the western portion falls under Oklahoma Territory.
- **Researcher note:** Before searching "Oklahoma" collections, determine whether your ancestors lived in Indian Territory (eastern, Five Tribes) or Oklahoma Territory (western, opened to non-Indian settlement 1889–1906), as the record sets differ significantly.

---

## Available Record Types

### Tribal Enrollment Rolls — THE Core Starting Point

These are the single most important record class for this place and period. The FamilySearch Wiki article on Oklahoma Native American Records ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)) identifies the following key rolls:

| Roll | Date | Tribe(s) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Old Settler Cherokee Roll** | 1851 | Cherokee | Named in FamilySearch Wiki |
| **Drennen Roll** | 1852 | Cherokee | Named in FamilySearch Wiki |
| **Dawes Rolls** | 1898–1914 | All Five Civilized Tribes | Most widely used; names, ages, sex, blood quantum, tribal affiliation |

- **Dawes Rolls** list name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation for enrolled members of the Five Civilized Tribes. Though they fall just after the mid-1800s target period, they are the entry point for nearly all Five Tribes genealogy and contain cross-references back to earlier rolls.
- **Access (Dawes Rolls):** Held at **NARA Fort Worth**; indexed on **FamilySearch** (collection 1987432: *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959*) and **Ancestry** — both searchable by name.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** imageGroupNumber **002298871** — *Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870* — 940 images, **99% name-indexed**, **full-text searchable**. Access level: **Indexed + images**. Reach it via FamilySearch record search or full-text search.

### Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* (Collection ID 1987432)
- 567,890 records / 283,945 images indexed
- Date range overlaps the entire target period
- Access level: **Indexed + images**
- URL: [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)

### Land Records

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* (Collection ID 1541872)
- 234,567 records / 117,283 images
- Covers the full mid-1800s window and extends to allotment-era records
- Land in Indian Territory was collectively held by tribal nations; individual allotments began with the Dawes Commission (post-1893). Pre-allotment records typically reflect tribal land assignments and improvements rather than fee-simple deeds.
- Access level: **Indexed + images**
- URL: [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)
- **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal land patents for the allotment era.

### Mission and Church Records

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* (Collection ID 1654321)
- 123,456 records / 61,728 images; date range begins before the target period
- **Denominations present** per FamilySearch Wiki ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)): Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian — all active in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward
- Missionary registers recorded converts, students, baptisms, marriages, and burials. These often capture individuals who never appear on a tribal roll.
- Access level: **Indexed + images**
- URL: [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)

### Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records

Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)), BIA records held at NARA include:
- **Annuity payment rolls** — list heads of household receiving treaty-guaranteed annuity payments; one of the best mid-century substitutes for a census
- **Agency correspondence** — may name individuals and describe family circumstances
- **Indian school records** — enrollment registers for reservation boarding and day schools

- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), primarily the Southwest Region (Fort Worth, TX) for Five Tribes records — [https://www.archives.gov/](https://www.archives.gov/)
- Access level: **Physical / microfilm** for most mid-1800s agency correspondence; some rolls digitized on Ancestry or FamilySearch

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

Indian Territory had no U.S. territorial civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during the mid-1800s. Each tribal nation maintained its own records, if any. Do not expect to find centralized birth/marriage/death registers comparable to a U.S. state during this period. The substitute sources are:
- Tribal rolls (enrollment data includes approximate ages and sometimes birth years)
- Missionary church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials)
- BIA agency records

### Census Records

Standard federal decennial censuses (1790–1880) did **not** include Indian Territory in the same enumeration as U.S. states and territories. Instead, look for:
- **Special Indian censuses** taken by tribal agents or the BIA — these appear in collection 1987432 (*Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959*) on FamilySearch
- **Dawes-era census cards** (volume 002298871, 1840–1870, 99% indexed)
- 1860 and 1880 federal censuses enumerated some non-Indian residents (federal employees, traders) living within Indian Territory — searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Military Records

- The Five Civilized Tribes had members who served in both Union and Confederate forces during the Civil War (1861–1865)
- **Fold3** ([https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/)) — curated as an external resource for this place; holds compiled military service records and pension files at NARA
- NARA holds compiled service records for "Indian Home Guards" (Union, Cherokee/Creek/Seminole units) and Confederate Indian Brigade units

### Probate and Court Records

- Each tribal nation maintained its own court system; probate jurisdiction resided with tribal courts, not U.S. courts
- U.S. federal courts for Indian Territory were established at various points; the U.S. Court for Indian Territory (headquartered at Muskogee from 1889) holds records relevant to the later period
- Tribal court records may be held at **tribal archives** or at NARA Fort Worth

### Cemetery Records

- **FindAGrave** ([https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/)) is listed as a curated external resource for this place. Coverage of Indian Territory rural and mission cemeteries varies widely — many graves were not formally recorded.
- Mission cemeteries associated with the denominational schools are sometimes documented in church records

### Newspaper Records

- **Newspapers.com** ([https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/)) is listed as a curated external resource. Mid-1800s Indian Territory newspapers are sparse but include the *Cherokee Phoenix* (pre-removal, Georgia) and later *Cherokee Advocate* (Tahlequah, 1844–); coverage in online databases should be verified directly.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Relevant Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* (1987432); *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* (1541872); *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* (1654321); Tribal Enrollment Cards vol. 002298871 | Free |
| **Ancestry** | Dawes Rolls; additional Indian Territory census and roll collections | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service records; pension files for Indian Territory units | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery transcriptions, varying coverage | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers including Cherokee-language papers | Subscription |

### Physical / Archival Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, TX** (archives.gov) | Dawes Rolls; BIA agency records; annuity rolls; correspondence; Indian school records; U.S. Court for Indian Territory records | In-person; many records also on microfilm or digitized |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City** | Tribal records, newspapers, photographs, territorial-era materials | In-person; some online |
| **Cherokee Nation Archives, Tahlequah, OK** | Cherokee tribal records, council minutes, land records | Contact tribe directly |
| **Five Civilized Tribes Museum / Tribal Archives** | Nation-specific records for Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole | Contact individual tribe |
| **Church/denominational archives** | Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian missionary registers | Contact denominations |

---

## Records NOT Online

- Most mid-1800s BIA agency correspondence and annuity rolls exist only on NARA microfilm or in physical form at Fort Worth
- Tribal court and probate records from tribal-government courts are held at NARA or tribal archives with very limited online access
- Individual tribal nation citizenship records (separate from the Dawes-era enrollment process) may exist only at tribal archives
- Many mid-century missionary station records not captured in the FamilySearch collection (1654321) remain in denominational archives

---

## Known Record Losses and Gaps

- The Civil War (1861–1865) caused significant destruction in Indian Territory; tribal government records, some mission records, and individual family papers were lost to the conflict. Treat this as a likely gap for records created between 1861 and 1865.
- Tribal nations were divided in their Civil War allegiances, and postwar reconstruction imposed new treaty requirements and new rolls — records created immediately after 1866 often reflect these upheavals.
- Standard federal census records (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) do not enumerate the Indian population of Indian Territory; the absence of a family in those censuses is expected, not a research failure.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the Dawes Rolls even if your ancestor died before 1898.** The Dawes enrollment process generated a "Cherokee by blood" or "Cherokee freedmen" card with cross-references to earlier rolls (Drennen, Old Settler, etc.) — working backward from a Dawes card often identifies the ancestor on a mid-century roll.
2. **Identify the specific tribal nation first.** Each of the Five Civilized Tribes kept separate records; searching across tribes without narrowing will waste time. Oral family tradition, death certificates, and obituaries are often the first clue to tribal affiliation.
3. **Annuity rolls are a census substitute.** For families between enumeration years, BIA annuity payment rolls list heads of household by name and sometimes list dependents — treat them like a mid-century census.
4. **Missionary records capture non-enrolled individuals.** Church baptismal and burial registers often recorded individuals who did not appear on any tribal roll, including freedpeople living among the tribes and mixed-heritage individuals.
5. **Blood quantum and enrollment disputes generate rich records.** If an ancestor was rejected from a roll or contested their enrollment status, the case file at NARA Fort Worth will contain genealogical affidavits, witness testimony, and family history — often the most detailed record that survives.
6. **The FamilySearch Wiki page on Oklahoma Native American Records** ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records)) is the best starting guide for this jurisdiction; the FamilySearch Wiki place pages for "Indian Territory" returned only generic content and are not a substitute.
7. **NARA's online catalog (catalog.archives.gov)** allows you to browse Record Group 75 (Records of the Bureau of Indian Affairs) by agency — search for the specific BIA agency that served your ancestor's tribe and location.

---

**Summary of digitization levels for target period (1830–1880):**

| Record Type | Digitization Level |
|---|---|
| Indian Censuses & Rolls (FS coll. 1987432) | Indexed + images |
| Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870 (vol. 002298871) | Indexed + images + full-text searchable |
| Early Land Records (FS coll. 1541872) | Indexed + images |
| Mission & Church Records (FS coll. 1654321) | Indexed + images |
| BIA annuity rolls / agency correspondence | Microfilm / physical only (NARA) |
| Tribal court / probate records | Physical only (NARA or tribal archives) |
| Mid-1800s newspaper runs | Partial — verify coverage on Newspapers.com |

---

This guide is grounded in the three FamilySearch collections, one digitized volume, and two FamilySearch Wiki article sections returned by the survey tools. The FamilySearch Wiki place pages for "Indian Territory, United States" returned only a generic fallback ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide)) rather than jurisdiction-specific content — consult the Oklahoma Native American Records article directly ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records)) for the most detailed wiki guidance on this topic.

---

## Pennsylvania Quaker Genealogy — Locality Research Guide
**Place:** Pennsylvania, United States | **Period:** Late 1700s (c. 1760–1800)
**Focus:** Religious meeting records and related Quaker genealogical sources

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania was founded in 1682 by Quaker William Penn as a haven for the Religious Society of Friends. By the late 1700s, Quakers were concentrated most heavily in **Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties**, with significant meetings also in Montgomery County (created 1784 from Philadelphia County) and York, Lancaster, and Cumberland counties along the frontier. Philadelphia Yearly Meeting served as the umbrella organization overseeing all monthly and quarterly meetings in the colony and early state.

**Critical registration context:** Pennsylvania did not mandate *statewide* civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until **1906**. For the late 1700s, Quaker meeting records are not supplementary — they are effectively *the* vital records for Quaker families. This makes them indispensable and, fortunately, unusually detailed.

---

### 🏆 Primary Source: Quaker Meeting Records

Quaker monthly meetings kept the most meticulous vital registers of any denomination in colonial America. What each record type captures:

| Record Type | What It Documents | Research Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Birth/death registers** | Name, date, parents' names | Substitutes for civil birth/death certificates |
| **Marriage records** | Full marriage certificate signed by *all witnesses present* | Names entire extended community — an extraordinary FAN cluster in one document |
| **Certificates of removal** | Transfer of membership from one meeting to another, with origin and destination meeting named | Traces geographic movement — essential for families who migrated |
| **Disownment records** | Name, offense, date, outcome | Documents members who married outside the faith, took oaths, or served in the military; still names the individual |
| **Monthly meeting minutes** | Business, committee work, oversight decisions | Contextual evidence; often names members and their circumstances |

**Meeting hierarchy:** Monthly meetings → Quarterly meetings → Philadelphia Yearly Meeting. Records were kept at the monthly meeting level. Quarterly and yearly meeting minutes are broader but less genealogically specific.

---

### Repositories

#### 🔵 Friends Historical Library — Swarthmore College (Swarthmore, PA)
The largest single collection of American Quaker records. Holds original and microfilmed registers from dozens of Pennsylvania monthly meetings. Access is in-person and by appointment; some finding aids are online at **swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library**.
*(Named in the FamilySearch wiki: [Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records))*

#### 🔵 Quaker and Special Collections — Haverford College (Haverford, PA)
Second major repository; strong holdings in Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records and correspondence. In-person access; catalog online at **haverford.edu/library/special-collections**.
*(Named in the Wikipedia summary for [Quakers in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania))*

#### 🔵 Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia, PA)
Holds supplementary Quaker material alongside colonial Pennsylvania court, land, and tax records that support Quaker research. **hsp.org**

#### 🔵 Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives (Philadelphia, PA)
The administrative records of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting itself. **pym.org**

---

### Published Finding Aid: Hinshaw's Encyclopedia

**William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, 6 volumes** — abstracts birth, marriage, death, removal, and disownment entries from Pennsylvania monthly meetings. This is the fastest first-pass tool for any Quaker research in Pennsylvania and is widely available in genealogical society libraries and on FamilySearch.
*(Cited in the FamilySearch wiki: [Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts))*

---

### FamilySearch Digitized Collections (1760–1800 window)

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638) | 1708–1985 | 1,245,830 | 607,220 | **Indexed + images** |
| [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | 446,607 | **Indexed + images** |
| [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | 156,023 | **Indexed + images** |
| [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | — | **Indexed, no images** |

**Digitized volume (browse-only):**
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** — 145 images (FamilySearch image group 001188322). This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be read image by image. No search shortcut exists; plan to browse the full run for a relevant meeting period.

> ⚠️ The *Church and Town Records* collection (1,245,830 records) is your best FamilySearch starting point — it aggregates records from multiple denominations including Friends meetings. However, coverage of individual monthly meetings varies. A hit there should be confirmed against the original register at Swarthmore or Haverford.

---

### Supporting Records (Non-Meeting)

Because Quakers often avoided government entanglements, some record classes are thinner — but others are exceptionally rich:

- **Probate records** — Quakers made wills at high rates; the Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (above) covers from 1683. County-level probate files often name children, spouses, and executors.
- **Land / deed records** — Held at county courthouses; Quaker families in Chester, Bucks, and Philadelphia counties left dense deed trails. These are largely physical or microfilm only for this period — no single digitized FamilySearch collection emerged from the volume search.
- **Tax records (1760s–1790s)** — Pennsylvania assessed taxable inhabitants by county. These exist at the county and state level and can place a family geographically before and after the Revolution. Check the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** — includes some Quaker marriages compiled from meeting records.
- **1790 Federal Census** — the first federal enumeration; heads of household only, but places the family in a county at a fixed date.

---

### External Repositories & Online Resources

FamilySearch curates 6 external resources for Pennsylvania in this period. The general-purpose repositories confirmed:

- **Ancestry.com** — U.S. Federal Census and some Pennsylvania church record collections
- **FamilySearch Wiki** — [Pennsylvania Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records) is the best online summary of Quaker holdings
- **Find A Grave / BillionGraves** — Quaker burial grounds (often simple markers) may have cemetery transcriptions
- **Newspapers.com** — Limited for 1760–1800, but Philadelphia had active newspapers that ran notices
- **Fold3** — Revolutionary War pension and service files; note that most Quakers were disowned for military service, so these are *negative-evidence* sources — absence confirms pacifist standing
- **NARA** — Revolutionary War pension files and early federal land records

> **Quaker-specific online resource:** The **Quaker Meeting Records** database at Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) has an online catalog of what is held and what has been microfilmed. Start there before a physical visit.

---

### Researcher Quirks & Warnings

1. **Marriage outside the meeting = disownment, but still documented.** If an ancestor married a non-Quaker ("marrying out"), the meeting recorded the disownment. The record names the individual and the offense — don't skip disownment minutes assuming they mean no record exists.

2. **Certificates of removal are migration documents.** When a Quaker family moved — from Philadelphia County to Chester County, or from Pennsylvania to Ohio or the Carolinas — the originating meeting issued a certificate of removal. These name the individual, their family, and both meetings. They are the closest equivalent to a migration document you will find.

3. **Search the meeting, not just the county.** Quaker records are organized by monthly meeting, not by civil county. A family in Chester County might belong to Concord Monthly Meeting, Goshen Monthly Meeting, or Bradford Monthly Meeting. Identify the specific meeting using Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* before going to the original registers.

4. **Montgomery County didn't exist until 1784.** Records for families in that area before 1784 were created under Philadelphia County jurisdiction. Search Philadelphia County deed and probate records for pre-1784 events even if the family later appears in Montgomery County.

5. **Quakers rarely appear in Revolutionary War military records.** The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting formally opposed participation in the war. Absence from military records is expected and is itself genealogical evidence of continued Quaker membership (or disownment recovery).

6. **The *Church and Town Records* collection is aggregated.** It may not include every monthly meeting. A negative result there does not mean no record exists — go to Friends Historical Library's catalog for the specific meeting.

7. **New Jersey border.** Many Philadelphia-area Quaker meetings had members on both sides of the Delaware River. Burlington Monthly Meeting (New Jersey) was closely tied to Pennsylvania Friends. If Philadelphia-area research stalls, check Burlington and Gloucester county (NJ) meeting records as well.

---

### Recommended Search Sequence

1. **Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia*** — first-pass name check across abstracted meeting records
2. **FamilySearch: Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records** (collection 1401638) — indexed search
3. **FamilySearch: Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages** (collection 1502909) — for marriage events
4. **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume** (browse-only; image group 001188322) — for the 1750–1800 window
5. **Friends Historical Library catalog** (Swarthmore) — identify the specific monthly meeting and its microfilm/original holdings
6. **Pennsylvania Probate Records** (collection 1999196) — wills and estate files
7. **County deed records** (physical, county courthouse or PA State Archives) — land and property trail
8. **1790 Federal Census** — place the family geographically at the end of the target period

---

This is a strong research environment: Quaker records are among the best-documented religious records in colonial America, both primary repositories (Swarthmore, Haverford) are accessible, FamilySearch has a substantial indexed collection, and Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* gives you a rapid first pass. The main gap is that specific monthly meeting registers beyond the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes are largely physical or microfilm-only on FamilySearch — plan a visit or correspondence with Friends Historical Library for the deepest research.

---

# Locality Research Guide
## Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Industry Era (c. 1870–1900)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Allegheny County** was formed in 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties. Pittsburgh has been the county seat since the city's founding (incorporated 1816). For the 1870–1900 window, all records fall squarely within Allegheny County — no boundary splits to navigate. The steel mill towns of **Homestead, Braddock, Duquesne, and McKeesport** all lie within Allegheny County and share the same county-level record sources.

The late 1800s brought massive immigrant waves — Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers — making ethnic church records and naturalization documents especially critical for this period. ([Wikipedia: Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh))

---

### ⚠️ Critical Quirks to Know Before You Search

1. **Pennsylvania did NOT require statewide vital registration until 1906.** For 1870–1900, births and deaths in Pittsburgh were recorded at the **county level** (Allegheny County began local registration c. 1870 — earlier than the statewide mandate). For marriages, county-level licenses began 1885. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
2. **The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire.** Substitute with Pittsburgh city directories, state tax lists, and church records for that decade gap.
3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across multiple courts.** Any court of record could naturalize — check county, state, and federal courts.
4. **Company employment records are fragmentary.** Most steel firms did not maintain systematic employee archives; what survives is held at specialized repositories, not online.
5. **Ethnic parish records may be in non-English languages** — Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, or German. Original registers are at the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives; plan to read the source language or hire a translator.

---

### 1. 🏭 Industrial & Occupational Records *(the highest-priority source class for this research)*

These are the most distinctive records for the steel era and the least likely to be found on mainstream genealogy databases.

| Source | What It Contains | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Company employment records** | Hire dates, wages, job assignments, injury/death notices | **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh); **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** archives | Physical access; some finding aids online at heinzhistorycenter.org |
| **Union membership lists** | Names, local #, trade, sometimes nationality | **Heinz History Center**; union local archives | Physical; inquire directly |
| **State factory inspector reports** | Lists of workers injured or killed in mills; mill names, sometimes worker names | **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Physical; partially microfilmed |
| **Pittsburgh city directories** | Name, occupation, street address; annual volumes from 1813 | **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** (complete run) | Physical; Ancestry.com has digitized many volumes — see [Ancestry.com Census/Directory Collections](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| **Federal census occupation columns** | 1870, 1880, 1900 all record occupation; 1880 adds relationship/disability; 1900 adds immigration year | FamilySearch / Ancestry | Indexed and searchable online |

> **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki on Allegheny County confirms that the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives hold the primary industrial record survival for this era. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Allegheny County Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))

---

### 2. 📋 Census Records

| Record | Years | Key Fields for Steel Workers | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| U.S. Federal Census | 1870, 1880, 1900 | Occupation, birthplace, parents' birthplace (1880+), immigration year (1900) | **Indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| Mortality Schedules | 1870, 1880 | Deaths in prior year, cause, occupation | FamilySearch; Ancestry |
| 1890 Census | ⚠️ *Largely destroyed* | — | Use city directories and church records as substitutes |

> The 1880 and 1900 censuses are particularly powerful for industrial workers — recording occupation, nationality of parents, and (in 1900) the year of immigration. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Allegheny County Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))

---

### 3. 🏛️ Vital Records

| Record | Coverage | FamilySearch Collection | Records / Images | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Births & Deaths (county) | Allegheny County from c. 1870 | Not yet a distinct FS indexed collection for this period | Physical at county; microfilm at FS | Pre-statewide registration; completeness varies |
| Death Certificates (statewide) | 1906–1968 | [Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) | 4,218,763 records + images | **Post-dates target period** — use for children/grandchildren born in steel era |
| Marriage Licenses | 1885–1950 | [Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | 524,189 records; images present | County courthouse records; Allegheny Co. from 1885 |
| Civil Marriages | 1677–1950 | [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 312,045 records; images present | Overlaps target window |
| Compiled Marriages | 1700–1900 | [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 198,765 records; **no images** | Index only; verify against originals |

---

### 4. ⛪ Church Records *(often the best source for immigrant families)*

The ethnic Catholic parishes of Pittsburgh's mill neighborhoods are genealogically irreplaceable — they often recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials more consistently than civil authorities for the 1870–1900 period.

| Source | Coverage | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Catholic ethnic parishes (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish) | Baptism, marriage, burial registers from 1840s onward | **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** holds originals; FamilySearch has microfilmed many | Physical at Diocese; microfilm/digital at FamilySearch |
| FamilySearch: Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records | 1708–1985 | [Collection 1401638](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638) | 1,245,830 records; 607,220 images | Indexed + images; search by name |
| German Lutheran, Reformed, Episcopal churches | Baptism/burial registers | **Heinz History Center**; denominational archives | Physical |

> ⚠️ Ethnic parish registers for Slovak, Polish, Croatian, and Italian congregations are often written in those languages (and sometimes in Latin for sacramental entries). The Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives is the primary custodian. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Allegheny County Vital & Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))

---

### 5. 🚢 Immigration & Naturalization

| Record | Coverage | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Passenger lists (port of arrival) | 1820–1957 | NARA; Ancestry; FamilySearch | Indexed online; [Ancestry Census/Immigration](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| Naturalization — Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas | 1798–1930 | **National Archives at Philadelphia** | Physical; some microfilm; partially indexed |
| Naturalization — federal courts | Pre/post-1906 | National Archives at Philadelphia | Physical |
| Declarations of intention ("first papers") | Any court pre-1906 | Multiple county and federal courts | Check Allegheny County Courthouse AND federal records |

> Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in ANY court of record — county courts of common pleas, federal district courts, or even city courts. Always check multiple courts. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Allegheny County Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))

---

### 6. 📜 Probate & Land Records

| Record | Coverage | FamilySearch Collection | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Probate (wills, estates, inventories) | 1683–1994 | [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | 893,214 records + 446,607 images; indexed |
| Deeds & land transfers | From 1788 (county formation) | Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds | Physical; some digitized via county portal |
| Tax assessment lists | Annual | Pennsylvania State Archives; county | Physical; pre-1800 lists on microfilm |

---

### 7. 📰 Newspapers & Military

| Record | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Pittsburgh newspapers (Pittsburgh Gazette, Pittsburgh Post) | Obituaries, labor strikes, workplace accident reports — especially valuable for documenting mill deaths | [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/); Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh microfilm holdings |
| Civil War pension files | Workers who served 1861–65; pensions extend well into the 1870s–1900s | [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/); NARA; [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/) |
| Cemetery records | Ethnic and municipal cemeteries in Pittsburgh | [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) |

---

### 8. Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | What They Hold | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) | Industrial/company records, immigration records, city directories, photograph collections | heinzhistorycenter.org; in-person research room |
| **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** | Steel industry archives, mill photographs, union records | riversofsteel.com; by appointment |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | Complete run of Pittsburgh city directories (1813+), local history, newspapers | carnegielibrary.org; in-person; some digitized |
| **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Ethnic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) | By appointment; diocesan archives office |
| **National Archives at Philadelphia** | Allegheny County naturalizations (1798–1930), federal court records, census microfilm | archives.gov/philadelphia |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Marriage licenses (1885+), birth/death registration (from 1870), deeds, court files | In-person; some indexes online via county website |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** | State factory inspector reports, military records, land office records, statewide records | phmc.pa.gov; in-person and microfilm |
| **FamilySearch.org** | See collections above; also microfilm of church and county records | Free online; some require Salt Lake City library visit |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, city directories, passenger lists, military records | Subscription; [ancestry.com/search/collections/census/](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |

---

### Digitization Coverage Summary

| Record Type | Digitization Level |
|---|---|
| Federal census (1870, 1880, 1900) | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885–1950 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania Church & Town Records | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania Probate Records | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania Death Certificates (1906+) | ✅ Indexed + images (post-period) |
| Allegheny County births/deaths 1870–1906 | ⚠️ Microfilm / physical only (no distinct indexed FS collection found for this window) |
| Company employment records | ❌ Physical only — Heinz History Center, Rivers of Steel |
| Union membership lists | ❌ Physical only |
| Naturalization records (pre-1906) | ⚠️ Partial — some microfilm; physical at NARA Philadelphia |
| State factory inspector reports | ❌ Physical only — Pennsylvania State Archives |
| Pittsburgh city directories | ⚠️ Partial — Ancestry has many volumes; Carnegie Library has complete run |

---

### Recommended Research Sequence

1. **Federal census 1880 and 1900** (FamilySearch/Ancestry) — establish occupation, address, and immigration year
2. **Pittsburgh city directories** (Carnegie Library or Ancestry) — track residence and job across the 1890 census gap
3. **Church records** at Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives — especially for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, and Irish families
4. **Naturalization records** at National Archives Philadelphia — declarations of intention and petitions
5. **Heinz History Center / Rivers of Steel** for company and union records — physical visit or inquiry required
6. **Newspapers.com** for mill accident reports and obituaries in Pittsburgh papers
7. **Pennsylvania County Marriages and Probate** on FamilySearch for civil record layer

## Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — Locality Research Guide
### Researching Families Affected by the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic
**Jurisdiction:** Philadelphia City & County, Pennsylvania, United States (co-terminus since 1682)
**Target period:** ~1780–1810 (bracketing the August–November 1793 epidemic)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Philadelphia city and county are **co-terminus** — records appear under both names, so search both. In 1793 Philadelphia was the U.S. capital and largest city, with roughly 50,000 residents. The epidemic killed approximately **5,000 people** (one-tenth of the population); thousands more fled to surrounding counties. Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil death registration** in 1793 — that did not begin until 1 January 1906. Church burial registers and specially compiled epidemic accounts are therefore the **primary death evidence** for this period.

---

### Tier 1 — Epidemic-Specific Records *(unique to the 1793 outbreak)*

| Record | What it names | Where held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mathew Carey, *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793)** | Published list of the dead, relief recipients, and escapees | HSP; digitized copies on Internet Archive and HathiTrust | Free online |
| **Committee of Citizens minutes & reports** | Names of relief recipients, orphans, the dead, and nurses | Philadelphia City Archives; HSP | Physical; some transcribed |
| **Bush Hill Hospital records** | Admitted patients and deaths at the epidemic's dedicated hospital | Philadelphia City Archives | Physical |
| **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's papers** | Official correspondence naming affected households | HSP | Physical |
| **Dr. Benjamin Rush's case notes & letters** | Patient names and treatments | Library Company of Philadelphia; HSP | Physical; some published |

> **Research tip:** Carey's account is the single fastest starting point — it names hundreds of dead and is fully digitized. Wikipedia's article on the epidemic ([https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)) names the primary repositories.

---

### Tier 2 — Church Records *(the main substitute for absent civil registration)*

Pennsylvania statewide vital registration began in 1906; for 1793, **church burial registers are the primary death record**. The FamilySearch collection **Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985** (collection ID 1401638; ~982,000 indexed persons, 607,000 images) is the best single starting point: [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638) — **indexed with images** (high access level).

The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** (GSP) has compiled separate indexes to many Philadelphia church registers not fully represented on FamilySearch. Philadelphia's major congregations active in 1793 include:

| Congregation | Denomination | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Christ Church** | Anglican/Episcopal | Large burial register; published transcription available |
| **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes')** | Lutheran/Swedish | One of the oldest continuous registers in PA |
| **St. Michael's & Zion** | German Lutheran | Records in German; GSP index available |
| **St. Mary's** | Roman Catholic | Earliest Catholic parish in PA |
| **Philadelphia Monthly Meeting** | Quaker | Meeting records at Haverford College & Swarthmore; extensive; non-burial "disownment" and removal records document fleeing families |
| **First Presbyterian** | Presbyterian | |
| **St. George's Methodist Episcopal** | Methodist | Oldest Methodist church in the US |
| **German Reformed Church** | Reformed | Records in German |
| **Mikveh Israel** | Jewish | Cemetery records survive |

> **Quirk:** German-congregation registers (St. Michael's & Zion, German Reformed) are in German — the researcher must read the original language or obtain a transcription.

> **Quirk:** Quaker records do **not** record baptisms or burials in the traditional sense; look instead for "burial minutes," removal certificates, and disownment entries in monthly meeting records. The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records are held at Haverford College and Swarthmore College's Friends Historical Library and are **not** fully on FamilySearch.

---

### Tier 3 — Civil & Government Records

#### Federal Census
The **1790 Federal Census** (three years before the epidemic) and **1800 Federal Census** bracket the event. Comparing household compositions can document deaths — a household present in 1790 with a widow or orphans in 1800 is a strong indicator of epidemic loss. Both censuses are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com.

#### Probate Records
The epidemic caused a **sharp spike in probate filings** in fall 1793. The FamilySearch collection **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection ID 1999196; ~893,000 records, 446,000 images) is **indexed with images**: [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196). Wills and estate inventories name heirs, creditors, and household property — invaluable when a head of household died suddenly. Philadelphia County orphans' court records (guardianships for epidemic-orphaned children) are held at the **Philadelphia City Archives**.

#### Marriage Records
Two FamilySearch collections cover pre-1810 marriages:
- **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** (col. 1571957; 312,000 records, 156,000 images) — indexed with images: [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)
- **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** (col. 1502909; 198,000 records, **no images**) — index only, no originals online: [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)

> **Note:** Pennsylvania's statewide county marriage registration began in 1885 — the 1793-era entries in the above collections derive from church records and published compilations, not civil registers.

#### Tax Records
Philadelphia city and county tax assessment lists survive for 1779–1793 and beyond. A family appearing in 1793 tax rolls but absent in 1794–1795 may have died or fled. Held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and **Pennsylvania State Archives**; limited digitization.

#### Land & Deed Records
Philadelphia County deed books are held at the **Philadelphia City Archives**. Rapid property transfers in late 1793–1794 may signal epidemic deaths. Limited digitization; physical access required.

---

### Tier 4 — Newspapers & Published Accounts

Philadelphia had several active newspapers in 1793 that published **death notices and obituaries**: *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, *General Advertiser*, and *Philadelphia Gazette*. Death notices for prominent residents are common; working-class individuals less so. Access via:
- **Newspapers.com** ([https://www.newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)) — subscription
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free) — limited 1793 coverage but worth checking
- **HSP newspaper collection** — physical holdings

---

### Tier 5 — Records of Fleeing Families

Thousands left Philadelphia in summer–fall 1793 and sheltered in the surrounding countryside. If your family is absent from Philadelphia records during this period, search:

- **Chester County, PA** (west) — Chester County Archives
- **Montgomery County, PA** (north/northwest) — Montgomery County Historical Society
- **Bucks County, PA** (north/northeast) — Bucks County Historical Society
- **Delaware County, PA** (southwest) — Delaware County Historical Society
- **Burlington County, NJ** (across the Delaware River) — New Jersey State Archives

Church records and tavern/inn registers in these counties occasionally document Philadelphia refugees. The **Pennsylvania State Archives** holds county-level tax and assessment records for all surrounding counties.

---

### Tier 6 — Military Records *(for men of military age)*

Many Philadelphia residents had served in the Revolutionary War (1775–1783). Pension files and bounty land warrants often survive the man and may document family structure:
- **NARA Revolutionary War pension files** — many are digitized on Fold3 ([https://www.fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) and Ancestry
- **Pennsylvania Archives Series** (published volumes) — muster rolls, pay abstracts, and militia records for Pennsylvania soldiers; available at HSP and on HathiTrust

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | City government records, orphans' court, deeds, early death returns, Committee of Citizens papers | Physical; some records digitized |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Manuscript collections, diaries, newspapers, published epidemic accounts, church record transcriptions | Physical + some digital via HSP Digital Library |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** | Indexes to Philadelphia church records; published in *Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine* | Physical + subscription database |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** | County tax records, state-level records | Physical; select records on Ancestry |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Digitized/indexed collections above; Philadelphia microfilm holdings | Free online |
| **Haverford College / Swarthmore Friends Library** | Quaker meeting records | Physical; finding aids online |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** | Rare printed materials, Rush papers, colonial newspapers | Physical |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal census, military records | Physical + Ancestry/Fold3 |

---

### Digitization Level Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Access Level |
|---|---|
| Church & Town Records (incl. burials) | **Indexed + images** (col. 1401638) |
| Probate Records | **Indexed + images** (col. 1999196) |
| Civil Marriages | **Indexed + images** (col. 1571957) |
| Compiled Marriages | **Index only, no images** (col. 1502909) |
| 1790 & 1800 Federal Census | **Indexed + images** (Ancestry & FamilySearch) |
| County death certificates | Not available until 1906 |
| Tax records | **Physical or microfilm only** (limited digitization) |
| Deed records | **Physical only** |
| Quaker meeting records | **Physical** (Haverford/Swarthmore); partial FamilySearch microfilm |
| Epidemic-specific (Carey, Committee) | **Free online** (Internet Archive, HathiTrust) or physical (HSP) |

---

### Research Strategy Summary

1. **Start with Mathew Carey's published account** (free on Internet Archive) — the fastest way to confirm whether a name appears among the documented dead.
2. **Search FamilySearch collection 1401638** (Church and Town Records) for burial entries in the family's denomination in fall 1793.
3. **Pull probate records** (col. 1999196) for anyone who died — wills filed in late 1793 or 1794 are particularly diagnostic.
4. **Compare the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses** to document household changes.
5. **Contact HSP and the Philadelphia City Archives** for Committee of Citizens records, Bush Hill hospital records, and manuscript sources not yet digitized.
6. **Check surrounding county records** (Chester, Montgomery, Bucks, Delaware, Burlington NJ) if the family fled the city.
7. **Consult GSP indexes** if the family's congregation isn't well covered on FamilySearch — particularly for German Lutheran, German Reformed, and smaller denominations.

# Locality Research Guide
## Chicago (Cook County), Illinois — Great Chicago Fire Era, c. 1840–1900

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Chicago is the seat of **Cook County**, Illinois (county established 1831; Illinois became a state in 1818). By October 1871, Chicago was the nation's fastest-growing city with roughly 300,000 residents — a major hub for German, Irish, Scandinavian, and Eastern European immigration.

The **Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871** is the defining records event for this jurisdiction. The fire destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles of the city, killed ~300 people, and left more than 100,000 homeless. Most critically for genealogists, the **Cook County Courthouse burned**, destroying:

- Deeds and land transfer records
- Pre-fire birth and death registers
- Most probate files
- Many court records (including some naturalization files)
- Tax rolls
- Many church registers in the burned district

**The research strategy divides sharply at October 1871.** Before the fire, you are working with substitutes. After the fire, county-level records restart and survive well.

---

## What Was Destroyed vs. What Survived

| Status | Record Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ❌ **Destroyed** | Pre-1871 county vital records | Birth/death registers at the Courthouse |
| ❌ **Destroyed** | Pre-1871 deeds and land records | Courthouse |
| ❌ **Destroyed** | Most pre-1871 probate files | Courthouse |
| ❌ **Destroyed** | Many church registers | Parishes within the burn zone |
| ❌ **Destroyed** | Pre-1871 tax rolls | Courthouse |
| ✅ **Survived** | Federal census (1840–1870) | Originals in Washington, D.C. — not in Chicago |
| ✅ **Survived** | City directories (from 1839) | Newberry Library; distributed copies pre-date fire |
| ✅ **Survived** | Some Cook County naturalization records | Circuit Court & Superior Court, from the 1840s |
| ✅ **Survived** | Church registers outside the burn zone | Denomination-specific |
| ✅ **Reconstructed** | Deeds re-filed under Burnt Record Act (1872) | Partial; owners had to voluntarily re-register |
| ✅ **Survived** | Insurance records (Chicago Title and Trust) | Chicago History Museum |

*Sources: Wikipedia "Great Chicago Fire"; FamilySearch Wiki "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy#Great_Fire" — [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)*

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 1. Vital Records
**Illinois statewide** civil registration did not begin until **1916** (compliance improving through the 1920s). Cook County began **local** registration in **1871** — but all pre-fire county vital records were destroyed.

**FamilySearch digitized collections (name-indexed, searchable):**
- **Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940** — 1,450,000 records
- **Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947** — 980,000 records
- **Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920** — 620,000 records

All three collections begin at 1871 — the practical floor for local civil vital records after the fire. For anything earlier, see Substitute Sources below.

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki "Illinois Vital Records#Statewide_Registration" — [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration)*

---

### 2. Census Records — Your Most Powerful Pre-Fire Sources

| Census | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1840 federal | ✅ Survived | Chicago's first enumeration |
| 1850 federal | ✅ Survived | Name-indexed on FamilySearch & Ancestry |
| 1860 federal | ✅ Survived | Name-indexed |
| **1870 federal** | ✅ **Survived** | **Your most valuable pre-fire snapshot** — taken just 15 months before the fire; originals were in Washington, D.C. |
| 1865 Illinois state census | Fragments only | Illinois State Archives, Springfield |
| 1880 federal | ✅ Survived | |
| **1890 federal** | ❌ **Destroyed** | A separate 1921 fire at NARA destroyed this nationwide — no Chicago substitute |
| 1900 federal | ✅ Survived | |
| Mortality schedules 1850–1880 | Partial | Death records for the year prior to each census; on FamilySearch and Ancestry |

**Key tip:** The 1870 federal census lists every Chicago household member one year before the fire. It is the indispensable pre-fire anchor for families in this period.

---

### 3. Church Records
**FamilySearch collection (name-indexed):**
- **Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925** — 285,000 records

**Key repositories:**
- **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives:** Catholic parish registers, including post-fire reconstructions by parishes that survived or re-established
- Lutheran, Episcopal, and other denominational archives — check individual denomination archives

**⚠️ Caution:** Church registers within the burn zone were often destroyed alongside civil records. Always determine whether your ancestor's specific parish was in the fire's path. Post-fire parishes re-established registers from 1871 onward; some surviving parishes outside the burn zone have continuous records.

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy#Repositories" — [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)*

---

### 4. Land and Property Records

Pre-1871 deeds were destroyed in the Courthouse. Two paths forward:

**A. Burnt Record Act (1872) reconstructed deeds:**
- Illinois legislation required property owners to re-file deeds after the fire
- **FamilySearch Volume 009982111** — "Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880": 112 images, **41% name-indexed** (partial name search available on FamilySearch), not full-text searchable — browse the unindexed remainder image by image
- **FamilySearch Volume 009982110** — "Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871": 38 images, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image by image with no search capability

**B. Insurance abstracts:**
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company records** at the Chicago History Museum partially substitute for destroyed deeds — these abstract chains of title that pre-date the fire

**⚠️ The Burnt Record Act is not a complete reconstruction.** Only property owners who voluntarily re-filed appear; some families are absent entirely.

---

### 5. Probate Records

Most pre-1871 Cook County probate files were destroyed. Post-1871 Cook County Circuit Court probate records are held at the **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University**. FamilySearch has microfilmed selected post-fire Cook County records.

---

### 6. Naturalization Records

Cook County naturalization records from the **Circuit Court and Superior Court** survive from the 1840s — some naturalization records appear to have survived or been partially reconstructed despite the courthouse fire. Pre-1906, naturalizations could be filed in any court of record (federal, state, or local).

- **Post-1906:** NARA Great Lakes Region facility (Chicago)
- Chicago was a major immigrant processing hub; search for port-of-arrival passenger lists separately (most immigrants entered via New York's Castle Garden or Ellis Island)

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki "Illinois Vital Records#Substitute_Records" — [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records)*

---

### 7. City Directories — A Critical Substitute Source

Chicago city directories were published from **1839** and survive the fire (as distributed copies, not held only at the Courthouse). They name residents with address and occupation — often the only pre-1871 documentation of a household's existence.

- **Newberry Library (Chicago):** The most comprehensive collection from 1839 onward
- Some directories are digitized on **Ancestry.com**

---

### 8. Newspapers — Fire Relief Lists and Obituaries

The **Chicago Tribune** (founded 1847) survived the fire and immediately published lists of fire victims, homeless residents, and relief recipients — naming thousands of affected families. This is often the only direct record that a specific family was caught in the fire.

| Resource | Access |
|---|---|
| Chicago Tribune (1847–) | Newspapers.com (subscription); ProQuest Historical |
| **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) | **Free** — [https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) |
| Newspapers.com | Subscription — [https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/) |

---

### 9. Fire Relief Records

The **Chicago Relief and Aid Society** distributed aid to displaced families and maintained detailed recipient lists. These records effectively document survivors by name, household, and circumstance — a genealogical windfall for families in the burn zone. Likely held at the **Chicago History Museum**.

---

### 10. Military Records

Illinois sent ~260,000 men in the Civil War (1861–1865).
- Service records and pension files: **NARA, Washington, D.C.**
- Illinois adjutant general records: **Illinois State Archives, Springfield**
- Digitized service records: **Fold3.com** — [https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/)

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** (Chicago) | City directories (1839–), maps, manuscripts, newspapers | In-person; some items online |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance records; fire relief lists; personal papers; photographs | In-person research |
| **IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University** | Cook County court and county records (post-1871) | In-person; some digitized |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers | By appointment |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person and partial online |
| **Illinois State Archives, Springfield** | Military records, state census fragments, land patents, death index (1916–) | In-person; some online at ilsos.gov |
| **NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago)** | Post-1906 naturalizations; federal records | In-person |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Church records, Cook County vital records (1871+), microfilm | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, city directories, vital records | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records | Free — [https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/) |

---

## Research Quirks and Warnings

1. **The "1871 wall"** — nearly all Cook County civil records restart in late 1871. Pre-fire research requires layering substitutes: 1870 census + city directories + church registers + naturalization records.
2. **Illinois statewide vital registration didn't begin until 1916** — Cook County's local registration from 1871 is the earliest civil vital record source, still wiped clean before that date by the fire.
3. **The 1870 census is your most critical document** — taken 15 months before the fire, it captures household members, birthplaces, and occupations. Always start here.
4. **The 1890 census is also lost** — a separate 1921 NARA fire destroyed it nationwide, creating a 20-year census gap (1880–1900). Bridge it with city directories, state census fragments, and church records.
5. **Burnt Record Act deeds are incomplete** — only owners who voluntarily re-filed appear; absence does not mean the family didn't own property before 1871.
6. **Two FamilySearch volumes cover the fire-era property gap:** Volume 009982110 (pre-fire reconstructed court records, 0% indexed) must be browsed image by image — no name search is possible. Volume 009982111 (post-fire re-recordings, 41% indexed) offers partial name search but requires browsing the remaining ~60%.
7. **Church records vary by parish location** — a parish in the burn zone almost certainly lost its registers; a parish one mile away may have continuous records from the 1840s. Locate the parish geographically before assuming records are gone.
8. **Chicago Relief and Aid Society records** may document your ancestor as a named fire survivor — check the Chicago History Museum.
9. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered** across multiple Cook County courts — check both Circuit Court and Superior Court series.
