## Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1699–1762) Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional Overview

**French Louisiana** (*La Louisiane*) was an administrative district of New France, with France controlling the territory from 1682 through 1762. The colony was anchored at New Orleans (founded 1718) and administered by the **Superior Council** (*Conseil Supérieur*). In **1762**, France secretly ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau), and the British received the eastern portion. Spain formally took administrative control ca. 1769.

> ⚠️ **Critical jurisdictional note:** The "1700s" straddles two colonial regimes. If your ancestors were alive after 1762, you must search **both French and early Spanish colonial records** — they are different administrative systems with different record-keepers, held in different archives. This guide covers the French period (1699–1762); Spanish colonial records (ca. 1762–1800) are a separate but closely linked research trail.

---

### 1. Catholic Parish Registers — **PRIMARY SOURCE**

**What they are:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials. The Catholic Church was the *only* legally recognized church in French Louisiana. The **Code Noir** (*Black Code*) required the Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, making parish registers among the very few record sources that name enslaved individuals in this period.

**Earliest records:** St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) registers begin **1720**.
*(Source: [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))*

**FamilySearch digitized collection:**
- 📂 **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** — Collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)
  - ~987,654 records; ~493,827 images
  - Covers the entire French colonial period from 1718 onward
  - *Indexing level: Cannot be confirmed without volume-level data, but the collection is searchable on FamilySearch — start here*

**Physical/original holdings:** Diocese archives and individual parish records held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans).

> ⚠️ **Language warning:** All French colonial parish registers are written in **French**. Researchers must be able to read 18th-century French script, or engage a translator.

---

### 2. Superior Council (*Conseil Supérieur*) Records — COURT, ESTATE & CONTRACTS

**What they are:** The governing body of French Louisiana produced land grants (*concessions*), court proceedings, contracts, and **estate inventories** — these are genealogically rich for identifying family members, property, debts, and relationships.

**Repository:** **Louisiana Historical Center**, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans. These records have been **partially digitized** but are not fully name-indexed.
*(Source: [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))*

**Access:** Contact the Louisiana Historical Center directly; some records are browsable at the Louisiana Secretary of State's archives portal.

> ⚠️ Browse-only risk: Partial digitization means many volumes must be searched image-by-image with no name index. Plan for in-person or image-browse research.

---

### 3. New Orleans Notarial Archives — WILLS, CONTRACTS, MARRIAGE SETTLEMENTS

**What they are:** The **oldest continuous notarial office in North America**, holding contracts, wills, marriage settlements (*contrats de mariage*), and property transactions **from the 1730s onward**. French civil law required notarial documentation for many transactions that English common law left unrecorded, making this archive exceptionally rich.
*(Source: [Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))*

**Repository:** **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — provides public access.
*(Source: [Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))*

> ✅ This archive is one of the most underused and most rewarding sources for French colonial Louisiana families.

---

### 4. Land Records — GRANTS & CONCESSIONS

**What they are:** French colonial land grants (*concessions*) follow French civil law, not English common law. Later Spanish grants continued the pattern. These are documented in:
- **American State Papers: Public Lands** series (published; available on Ancestry, Google Books, and HathiTrust)
- **Louisiana State Land Office** records
*(Source: [Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))*

---

### 5. Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) — FRANCE

**What they are:** France's colonial administrative archive in **Aix-en-Provence** holds:
- Administrative correspondence between colonial governors and Versailles
- **Colonial census rolls** (*dénombrements*) enumerating settler households
- Military rosters and officer records
*(Source: [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))*

**Access:** The ANOM is accessible in person in Aix-en-Provence; some finding aids and select record images are available online at **[anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)**. This is the essential repository for records created at the colonial administration level — not replicated anywhere in the U.S.

> ⚠️ **Physical/overseas repository.** Most ANOM records are not digitized or name-indexed online. Budget for correspondence with the archive or a professional researcher in France.

---

### 6. Probate Records

**FamilySearch digitized collection:**
- 📂 **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** — Collection [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)
  - ~456,789 records; ~228,394 images
  - Starts at **1756**, reaching into the final years of French colonial administration
  - Wills, inventories, and administration records

---

### 7. Census Records

**Colonial census rolls** (*dénombrements*) were conducted sporadically under French rule and are held primarily at **ANOM** (France). No FamilySearch-indexed colonial census collection was identified in the tools' results for the 1700–1762 period. The first U.S. Federal Census (1790) postdates French rule entirely and covers Louisiana only from 1810 onward (after the Louisiana Purchase, 1803).

---

### 8. Military Records

French colonial military rosters and officer records are held at **ANOM** (France). No FamilySearch collection covering French Louisiana military records was returned by the survey. Researchers seeking French colonial soldiers or militia members should contact ANOM directly.

---

### 9. Slave and Enslaved Ancestry

The **Code Noir** required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, so parish registers (see §1 above) are the primary — and often only — genealogical source for enslaved ancestors in this period. Estate inventories in Superior Council and notarial records also name enslaved individuals. The Louisiana Historical Center's collections of Superior Council records are particularly important for this research.

---

### Key Research Quirks & Warnings

| | |
|---|---|
| 🌐 **French → Spanish transition** | Records created after ca. 1762–1769 shift from French to Spanish administration. If your ancestors span both periods, you need both record systems. |
| 🇫🇷 **Language** | All French colonial records are in French; many require reading 18th-century manuscript script. |
| 🏛️ **No U.S. civil registration** | Civil registration of vital events did not exist in the French colonial period. Catholic parish registers are the substitute. |
| 📍 **Parish-level geography** | Louisiana used Catholic ecclesiastical parishes (not counties) as the primary civil division — records are organized by parish, not county. |
| 🔍 **Notarial records are underused** | French civil law required notarization of many life events; the New Orleans Notarial Archives (from 1730s) hold a wealth of family data often overlooked by researchers focused only on church and probate records. |
| 📦 **ANOM is non-negotiable for colonial families** | Administrative records, census rolls, and military rosters at the ANOM in France cannot be found anywhere in the U.S. — consult it for any family present in Louisiana before 1762. |

---

### Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church Records 1718–1925; Probate 1756–1984 | Free online at familysearch.org |
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) | Superior Council records, partially digitized | In-person or contact archive |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives** | Contracts, wills, marriage settlements from 1730s | Public access, Research Center |
| **Louisiana State Land Office** | Colonial land grants | Online + in-person |
| **ANOM** (Aix-en-Provence, France) | Census rolls, administrative records, military | In-person or correspondence |
| **St. Louis Cathedral** (New Orleans) | Parish registers from 1720 | Diocese/Louisiana Historical Center |

---

### Coverage Gaps Noted

- The FamilySearch wiki_place_page tool returned only a **generic fallback** for all four Louisiana sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at **[familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy)** for supplementary guidance.
- The external links survey returned only generic genealogy sites (Ancestry, NARA, Find A Grave) rather than Louisiana colonial-specific links — the colonial-era repositories above are not well-represented in FamilySearch's curated external link set for this time window.
- **Volume-level indexing data** (how much of each FamilySearch collection is name-searchable vs. browse-only) could not be retrieved in this survey — treat FamilySearch collection record counts as estimates and test searchability directly on the site.
- No FamilySearch-indexed collection was found for **French colonial censuses or military records** — ANOM (France) is the path for those.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns (Late 1800s, c. 1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Pennsylvania's coal mining region divides into two distinct zones, each with its own county structure and record-keeping history:

**Anthracite (hard coal) — Northeastern PA:**
Schuylkill (formed 1811), Luzerne, Lackawanna (formed from Luzerne **1878**), Carbon (formed 1843), and Northumberland counties. This is the heartland of mining genealogy — Pottsville, Scranton, Wilkes-Barre, Mahanoy City, Shenandoah, Shamokin.

**Bituminous (soft coal) — Western PA:**
Cambria (formed 1804), Allegheny, Westmoreland, Fayette, Washington, and Indiana counties. Johnstown (Cambria County) is the major center.

**Economy:** Coal mining dominated; major employers included the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company, the Lehigh Valley Coal Company, and Pennsylvania Railroad coal subsidiaries. (*Wikipedia: Coal mining in Pennsylvania*, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_mining_in_Pennsylvania)

**Ethnic composition:** The workforce was heavily immigrant. Early waves (1840s–1860s) brought Irish (famine migration) and Welsh (skilled miners) and Germans. The "new immigration" of the 1880s–1890s added large numbers of Poles, Lithuanians, Slovaks, Italians, and Ukrainians. (*Wikipedia: Coal Region*, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region)

**Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian parishes), Welsh Congregational and Baptist, German Lutheran and Reformed, Anglican/Episcopalian, Eastern Catholic and Greek Catholic (for Slavic communities). Ethnic parishes often maintained records in their heritage language.

**Key events affecting records:** The Avondale Mine Disaster (1869) killed 110 men and prompted Pennsylvania's first mine safety legislation and the creation of the annual Mine Inspector Reports. The Molly Maguires trials (1875–1877) produced substantial court records. The founding of the United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) in 1890 created union membership records.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Lackawanna County** was carved from Luzerne County in **1878**. Records for Scranton, Carbondale, and surrounding areas *before 1878* are filed under **Luzerne County** — search Luzerne first for anything before that date. After 1878, search Lackawanna directly.
- **Carbon County** was formed in 1843; earlier records for that territory are in Northampton and Monroe counties.
- **Cambria County** was formed in 1804 from Somerset and Huntingdon counties.
- The anthracite-region counties were all established by mid-century and had stable boundaries through the late 1800s.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Critical gap:** Pennsylvania **did not require statewide registration of births and deaths until 1906.** Before that date, vital events for coal region families were recorded only by churches, in family Bibles, or (for two counties only) by Philadelphia County from 1860 and Allegheny County from 1870. Source: *Pennsylvania Vital Records* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)
- **Marriage records** are the exception: marriage licenses and bonds have been kept at the county courthouse from the colonial period onward. (*Pennsylvania Vital Records*, same source)
- **FamilySearch collections for marriages:**
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* — 524,189 records, 1,048,378 persons, 312,045 images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) — **indexed + images**
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* — 312,045 records, 156,023 images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) — **indexed + images**
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* — 198,765 records, **no images** (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) — **index only; no original images**
- **Death certificates (post-period):** Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 — 4,218,763 records with images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317). Though these postdate the late 1800s, death certificates for elderly miners dying after 1906 often give birthplace, parents' names, and immigration information useful for tracing back to Europe.
- **Pre-1906 death substitute:** Mine Inspector Annual Reports (see Occupational Records below) and church burial registers are the primary alternatives for deaths before 1906.

### Church Records
- **The single most important source for late-1800s coal region vital events.** Because Pennsylvania had no statewide birth/death registration during this period, ethnic parish registers are often the only record of births, marriages, and burials.
- **Denominations:** Irish and later Polish/Slovak/Lithuanian Catholic parishes; Welsh Congregational and Baptist; German Lutheran and Reformed; Eastern and Greek Catholic for Slavic immigrants.
- **Language warning:** Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, and Ukrainian parish registers of this era are commonly in Latin (sacramental entries) or in the congregation's heritage language. German Lutheran records may be in German. Be prepared to read the original language or obtain a translation.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985* — 1,245,830 records, 982,415 persons, 607,220 images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638) — **indexed + images** — covers many denominations across the state.
- **Physical holdings:** Original registers remain with individual parishes (if still active) or have been transferred to diocesan archives. The Diocese of Scranton archives and the Archdiocese of Philadelphia archives hold many transferred registers. FamilySearch has microfilmed a substantial portion.

### Census Records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1890 (mostly destroyed by fire and water), 1900 are the key enumerations for this period. The 1880 and 1900 censuses are fully indexed on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry. Occupation column records "miner" and helps identify mining families. Birthplace and parents' birthplace columns are critical for immigrant ancestry.
- **Mortality schedules** (1860, 1870, 1880) record deaths in the twelve months preceding the census — a valuable substitute for missing death records, especially for mine accident victims.
- **Pennsylvania state census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct state censuses during this period. The federal decennial census is the primary enumeration.
- **Access:** Indexed + images for 1860–1880 and 1900 on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). External links confirmed: *U.S. Federal Census Collection — Ancestry.com* (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Occupational Records — Coal Mining (Unique to This Region)
This is the record category that sets coal mining towns apart from other localities.

- **Mine Inspector Annual Reports (from 1870):** Published annually by the state after the Avondale disaster legislation. Each report lists **fatal mine accidents with the victim's name, age, nationality, and cause of death** — an invaluable substitute for missing death records. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). Source: *Pennsylvania Occupational Records* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill County, 1870–1900:** Digitized volume on FamilySearch — image group **002240015**, 410 images, **95% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — the most accessible mining-specific record on FamilySearch for this region. (**Indexed + images**)
- **Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne County, 1870–1895:** Image group **002240016**, 287 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image by image. (**Browse-only**)
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna County, 1878–1900:** Image group **002240017**, 199 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable** — browse-only. (**Browse-only**)
- **Note on total volume coverage:** The volume search returned 23 total volumes for Pennsylvania in this period; details on the 3 above come from the first page of results. Additional volumes (census, church, probate, land, etc.) are in the remaining pages — search FamilySearch's catalog directly for the full list.
- **Company employment records** survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties. Source: *Pennsylvania Occupational Records* (same URL).
- **UMWA union records (from 1890):** The United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) created membership rolls and grievance files. Contact the UMWA Archives at Indiana University of Pennsylvania.

### Probate and Court Records
- **Probate:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, and letters of administration at the county **Register of Wills** from each county's formation. FamilySearch collection: *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* — 893,214 records with 446,607 images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — **indexed + images**. Source: *Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **Naturalization records:** Before 1906, immigrants could naturalize in any court of record — county Court of Common Pleas, state court, or federal court. **Schuylkill County naturalization records from the 1840s through 1906 are at the Pennsylvania State Archives.** Source: *Pennsylvania Occupational Records* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources). Check county prothonotary offices and NARA's Philadelphia regional archives (National Archives at Philadelphia, 900 Market St.) for federal court naturalizations.

### Land Records
- Pennsylvania is a **state-land state** (not a federal public-land state). The Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records from William Penn's original grants (1681) onward. County deed books begin at each county's formation date and are held at the county Recorder of Deeds. Source: *Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)
- **Note for coal region research:** Many mining families rented company housing (patch towns) and never owned land — land records may have limited value for tenant miners. However, deeds *do* appear when miners purchased modest homes, and coal company land grants can document when and where mines operated.

### Tax Records
- Pennsylvania county assessment and tax records (called "tax duplicates") survive from the late 1700s in many counties. They serve as a **census substitute** and can track a family year-by-year between federal censuses. Held at county archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- Source: *Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records) notes survival from the 1690s in some counties; coal-region counties typically have assessments from their formation dates.

### Military Records
- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Many future coal miners served or were of service age. Pennsylvania raised 215+ regiments. Service records and pension files at NARA (Washington, DC); pension files especially rich for family information. *Military Records — Fold3* (https://www.fold3.com/) has Pennsylvania Civil War records.
- **Spanish-American War (1898):** Relevant for the end of the period. Service records at NARA.
- **State records:** Pennsylvania State Archives holds adjutant general records and muster rolls.

### Cemetery Records
- Mine disasters and accidents produced large numbers of deaths. Cemetery records are important both for death documentation and for identifying community clusters.
- **Online:** *Cemetery Records — Find A Grave* (https://www.findagrave.com/) — good coverage of many coal region cemeteries.
- **Physical:** Sexton records and burial registers remain with individual cemeteries (church-run or municipal) or local historical societies.

### Newspaper Records
- Coal region newspapers (Pottsville *Miners' Journal*, Scranton *Tribune*, Wilkes-Barre *Times*, etc.) carried obituaries, mine accident reports, inquest proceedings, marriage notices, and legal notices.
- **Online:** *Historical Newspapers — Newspapers.com* (https://www.newspapers.com/) has substantial Pennsylvania newspaper holdings. Chronicling America (free, Library of Congress) also covers some Pennsylvania titles.
- **Physical:** Pennsylvania State Library (Harrisburg) and local public libraries hold microfilm runs of regional papers.

### Immigration and Naturalization
- Most anthracite-region immigrants arrived through **Philadelphia** (Irish, Welsh, Germans early) or **New York** (all groups, especially post-1880 Poles, Lithuanians, Slovaks, Italians). Passenger lists are at NARA and indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- Naturalization petitions before 1906 were filed in county courts; after 1906, at federal district courts. Note that declaration of intent (first papers) and final petition (second papers) are separate documents filed potentially years apart and in different courts if a miner moved between counties.
- **Important:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine full manifests when tracing families.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Key holdings for this place/period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church & Town Records 1708–1985; County Marriages 1885–1950; Civil Marriages 1677–1950; Compiled Marriages 1700–1900; Probate Records 1683–1994; Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill, browse/indexed); Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne, browse-only); Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna, browse-only) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census 1860–1900; PA death certificates; naturalization records; passenger lists | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Civil War service and pension files; military records | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery transcriptions, coal region cemeteries | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | PA historical newspapers including coal region titles | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Federal court naturalization records; passenger lists; military records | Free to search; copies fee-based |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Mine Inspector Annual Reports (1870+); Schuylkill Co. naturalization records; state tax records; company employment records (fragmentary); state military records | In-person; some records online via PA Digital Collections |
| **National Archives at Philadelphia** | Federal court naturalization records; federal census originals; immigration records (Philadelphia port) | In-person; 900 Market St., Philadelphia |
| **County Courthouses** (Register of Wills, Recorder of Deeds, Prothonotary) | Probate (wills, administrations); deeds; naturalization petitions; marriage licenses | In-person or mail; contact each county office |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | Local mining records, newspapers, photographs, family files | In-person; check hours |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton) | Mining community records, company records, immigrant community materials for northeastern PA coal region | In-person; contact for research inquiries |
| **Diocese of Scranton Archives / Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives** | Transferred Catholic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) from dissolved or merged parishes | Contact for access |
| **Indiana University of Pennsylvania** | UMWA Archives — union membership rolls and grievance files (from 1890) | In-person; advance contact recommended |

---

## Records NOT Online

- **Mine Inspector Annual Reports (1870 onward):** Physical volumes at the Pennsylvania State Archives; not fully digitized or indexed online.
- **Most company employment records:** Fragmentary survival at PA State Archives and local historical societies — not systematically digitized.
- **Pre-1878 Lackawanna-area records (filed under Luzerne County):** Many probate, deed, and court records for Scranton/Carbondale before 1878 are in Luzerne County's physical record books — not fully online.
- **Ethnic church registers** not microfilmed by FamilySearch: Many Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, and Ukrainian parish registers from the 1880s–1890s remain with parishes or diocesan archives — not online.
- **Tax duplicates (county assessment records):** Generally physical-only at county archives or the PA State Archives.
- **UMWA union records:** Physical only at Indiana University of Pennsylvania.

---

## Known Record Losses and Gaps

- **1890 federal census:** Largely destroyed by fire and water damage in Washington, DC (1921). Only fragments survive nationally; none for the Pennsylvania coal counties in this guide. Substitute with 1880 and 1900 censuses, plus state/county tax records for the 1890s.
- **Vital records before 1906:** No statewide birth or death registration — this is a structural gap, not a loss. Church registers, census mortality schedules, Mine Inspector Reports, and newspaper obituaries partially compensate.
- **Company record losses:** Many mining company archives were not preserved when companies closed, merged, or were absorbed. What survives is fragmentary.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses** — they are fully indexed, free on FamilySearch, and will tell you a miner's birthplace, parents' birthplaces, and neighbors (who were often co-ethnic and sometimes kin).

2. **Lackawanna County records before 1878 are in Luzerne County** — if your ancestor lived in the Scranton area before 1878, search Luzerne County first for all record types (probate, deeds, marriages, court). Source: Wikipedia; confirmed by Lackawanna County formation date (+1878 from place_search).

3. **The Mine Inspector Annual Reports are the only systematic pre-1906 death record for miners** — if an ancestor died in the mines, this is where to look. PA State Archives, Harrisburg. Source: *Pennsylvania Occupational Records* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)

4. **Church records are your vital records for 1860–1906** — identify the specific ethnic parish your ancestor's community worshipped at. Irish and Welsh miners arrived earlier (1840s–1860s); Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, Italian, and Ukrainian immigrants arrived mostly 1880s–1900s, and their communities established new ethnic parishes. Check diocesan archives for registers not yet microfilmed.

5. **The Schuylkill Mine Worker Employment Cards (image group 002240015) are 95% name-indexed on FamilySearch and full-text searchable** — the most accessible occupational record for the region. Search this first if your ancestor worked in Schuylkill County.

6. **Naturalization records pre-1906 can be in any court** — check county Courts of Common Pleas, state courts, AND federal district court (National Archives at Philadelphia). Schuylkill County naturalization records 1840s–1906 are specifically noted at the PA State Archives. Source: *Pennsylvania Occupational Records* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)

7. **Pennsylvania is a state-land state** — land patents go through the Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg), not the federal Bureau of Land Management. Many miners rented company-owned patch-town housing and will not appear in deed records; look instead for the rare moment they purchased a home.

8. **Death certificates after 1906 are valuable for pre-1906 research** — an elderly miner dying in 1910 or 1920 will have a death certificate listing his birthplace, parents' names, and possibly immigration year. The FamilySearch collection *Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968* (4.2 million records, fully indexed) is a rich back-door into late-1800s biographical data.

9. **Ethnic mutual aid societies** (Polish National Alliance, Slovak Catholic Sokol, Ancient Order of Hibernians for Irish miners, etc.) created membership rolls, death benefit records, and fraternal newspapers — ask local historical societies what survives for specific towns.

10. **FamilySearch volume search found 23 digitized volumes** for Pennsylvania in this period — the guide above covers the first-page results. Search FamilySearch's catalog at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog for additional volumes by county (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Cambria) to discover the full set.

## 🗺️ Locality Research Guide: Early Massachusetts Puritan Settlements, c. 1620–1700

---

### JURISDICTIONAL CONTEXT

Early colonial Massachusetts comprised **two separate colonies** that must be searched independently:

| Colony | Dates | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Plymouth Colony** | 1620–1691 | Mayflower settlers; absorbed into Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691 |
| **Massachusetts Bay Colony** | 1628/1630–1691 | ~20,000 settlers in Winthrop's Great Migration, 1630–1640 |
| **Province of Massachusetts Bay** | 1691 onward | Unified province under new royal charter |

**Key structural dates that affect records:**
- **1639** — The General Court of Massachusetts Bay ordered all **towns** to record births, marriages, and deaths. This is town-level civil registration, not statewide — statewide registration did not begin until **1841**. Never cite "Massachusetts didn't require registration until 1841"; that erases 200 years of town records. *(Source: wiki_search, [Massachusetts Genealogy – Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))*
- **1643** — Four original counties formed: **Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, and Norfolk**. County-level court, probate, and deed records begin here. Records before 1643 are at the colony level.
- **1691** — Plymouth Colony absorbed; its records remain a separate corpus.

---

### RECORD TYPES & AVAILABILITY

#### 1. 📋 Town Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
- **Level:** Town | **Coverage:** 1639 onward (some towns earlier via church records)
- **FamilySearch:** ✅ **Indexed + images** — **Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** (Collection [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)) — 3,456,789 indexed records, 1,728,394 images
- **Published abstracts:** The *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* series (**Tanner–Corbin series**) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. Widely held at libraries and NEHGS. Use alongside originals. *(Source: wiki_search, [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))*
- ⚠️ **Gap:** The 1620–1639 window predates the town mandate. Rely on church records and compiled sources for those two decades.

---

#### 2. ⛪ Congregational Church Records
- **Level:** Individual congregation | **Coverage:** 1630s onward
- **FamilySearch:** ✅ **Indexed + images** — **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** (Collection [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)) — 987,654 indexed records, 493,827 images
- As the **established church of the colony**, Congregational meetings are the backbone of Puritan-era genealogy. Records include:
  - Membership lists (admissions and dismissals)
  - Baptisms, marriages, burials
  - **Disciplinary proceedings** (admonishments, excommunications) — often name spouses, parents, and neighbors
- Many early church records have been **published** by the **Colonial Society of Massachusetts** and local historical societies. *(Source: wiki_search, [Massachusetts Church Records – Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))*
- 💡 Search church membership lists, not just baptism/marriage registers — many families appear only there.

---

#### 3. ⚖️ Probate Records
- **Level:** County (from 1643); colony-level before 1643 | **Coverage:** 1635 onward
- **FamilySearch:** ✅ **Indexed + images** — **Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991** (Collection [1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)) — 567,890 indexed records, 283,945 images
- Wills, estate inventories, administration bonds, and guardianship files name heirs, children, and creditors — genealogically among the richest sources for this era. *(Source: wiki_search, [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))*
- Records before 1643 are at the **Massachusetts Archives** (colony level), not county courthouses.

---

#### 4. 📜 Land Records (Deeds & Grants)
- **Level:** County registries of deeds (from 1643); colony/town grants earlier | **Coverage:** 1630s onward
- **Digitization:** Physical and microfilm primarily — no dedicated FamilySearch indexed collection appeared in this survey
- Land deed books survive in **remarkably complete runs** at the four original county registries of deeds (Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, Norfolk). *(Source: wiki_search, [Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))*
- Early colony-era **land grants** are in colony records held at the **Massachusetts Archives**.
- 💡 Deeds place individuals in a town at a specific date and often name adjacent landowners (neighbors = potential relatives).

---

#### 5. 🏛️ Colonial Court Records
- **Level:** Colony (General Court) and county (Quarter Sessions) | **Coverage:** 1620s onward
- **Digitization:** Primarily physical and microfilm
- The **Massachusetts Archives** in Boston holds original colony records, Governor's correspondence, and court records from the 1620s onward. *(Source: wiki_search, [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))*
- General Court records (legislative/judicial) and county court files can name colonists in disputes, indentures, and civic proceedings.

---

#### 6. 🚢 Plymouth Colony Records (1620–1691)
- **Status:** Separate jurisdiction — **must be searched independently**
- Plymouth Colony records have been **published and indexed separately** from Massachusetts Bay Colony materials. *(Source: wiki_search, [Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))*
- Key published source: *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth in New England* (12 vols., ed. Shurtleff & Pulsifer) — available at major research libraries and Google Books.
- ⚠️ Never assume Massachusetts Bay Colony collections cover Plymouth families before 1691.

---

#### 7. 🛳️ Great Migration / Immigration (1620–1643)
- **No period-appropriate passenger list collection exists on FamilySearch** — the Massachusetts, Passenger Lists collection (1784312) begins in **1820** and is irrelevant for this period.
- The primary tool is the **NEHGS Great Migration Study Series**, which documents every known settler who arrived 1620–1643, including origins, ship, family members, and source citations. Published by NEHGS; accessible at [AmericanAncestors.org](https://www.americanancestors.org). *(Source: wiki_search, [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))*
- **Savage's** *Genealogical Dictionary of the First Settlers of New England* (4 vols.) — classic 19th-century compiled reference for thousands of colonial families.

---

#### 8. ⚔️ Military Records
- **Coverage:** Colonial militia, King Philip's War (1675–76), and later conflicts
- Some colonial militia muster rolls are at the Massachusetts Archives and NARA.
- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) and **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) hold relevant military records.
- King Philip's War (1675–1676) generated significant service documentation.

---

#### 9. 🪦 Cemetery Records
- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) indexes colonial-era gravestones from Massachusetts towns; Puritan cemeteries survive in many towns.
- Physical stones may predate formal burial registration.

---

### KEY REPOSITORIES

| Repository | Holdings for 1620–1700 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives**, Boston | Colony records, court records, land grants, governor's correspondence from 1620s | Physical + some digitized; sec.state.ma.us/arc/ |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)**, Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration Study Series; manuscripts; Tanner-Corbin vital records | Members online at [americanancestors.org](https://www.americanancestors.org); on-site research |
| **FamilySearch** | Town Vital Records (2061550), Church Records (1921657), Probate Records (1678901) | Free at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **County Registries of Deeds** (Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk, Norfolk) | Deed books from 1643 onward | Physical; some via state portal |
| **Colonial Society of Massachusetts** | Published series of church and colonial records | Major research libraries |
| **NARA** | Federal-level colonial records; military records | archives.gov |

---

### RESEARCH QUIRKS & CRITICAL GOTCHAS

1. **Town registration started 1639, not 1841** — The 1841 date is statewide registration. Town-level records go back to 1639; for the 1620–1638 gap, church records are the primary substitute.

2. **Plymouth Colony = separate search** — Its records were never folded into the standard Massachusetts collections. Always search Plymouth Colony sources independently for pre-1692 families.

3. **No counties before 1643** — Court, probate, and deed records before 1643 are colony-level documents at the Massachusetts Archives, not at county courthouses.

4. **No census records for this period** — Federal census begins in 1790. For population coverage, use: church membership lists, town tax lists, colonial militia musters, and the NEHGS Great Migration series.

5. **Congregational records are often more complete than town records** — Church membership lists survive for some families and periods where town vital registers have gaps.

6. **Bordering jurisdictions** — Families near Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Hampshire, or Maine may have records in those separate colonial governments. Maine was part of Massachusetts but kept as a distinct district (York County); check York County records as well.

7. **Published abstracts first, then originals** — The Tanner–Corbin vital records series, Great Migration Study Series, and Savage's *Dictionary* are mature scholarly tools. They are the fastest entry point and cite the originals you can then pull.

8. **The Great Migration passenger collection on FamilySearch (1784312) starts in 1820** — Do not use it for 1620–1700 arrivals.

---

### SUMMARY: WHERE TO START

| Research goal | First stop |
|---|---|
| Find a birth, marriage, or death | FamilySearch Collection 2061550 (Town Vital Records) + Tanner–Corbin series |
| Identify a Puritan family's church | FamilySearch Collection 1921657 (Church Records) + Colonial Society publications |
| Find a will or estate | FamilySearch Collection 1678901 (Probate Records) |
| Trace a Great Migration arrival | NEHGS Great Migration Study Series; Savage's Dictionary |
| Plymouth Colony ancestry | Published *Records of Plymouth Colony* (Shurtleff/Pulsifer) |
| Colonial land or court records | Massachusetts Archives, Boston (physical) |

Massachusetts is one of the best-documented early colonial regions in North America — the combination of the 1639 town-registration mandate, robust church recordkeeping, and NEHGS scholarship means that Puritan families are often traceable with surprising depth.

# Oklahoma Land Run Research Guide (1889–c. 1920)

## Jurisdictional Context

The Land Run of 1889 opened the "Unassigned Lands" of central/western Oklahoma on April 22, 1889, with ~50,000 participants staking claims on ~2 million acres. Land offices at Guthrie and Kingfisher processed the original homestead applications. The territorial government followed on May 2, 1890 (Organic Act), and statehood came November 16, 1907, when Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged.

**The single most important research decision is identifying which territory your ancestor lived in before 1907:**

| Period | Jurisdiction | Record Authority |
|--------|-------------|-----------------|
| Apr. 22 – May 1, 1890 | Unassigned Lands (no territorial govt.) | Federal General Land Office only; almost no local records |
| May 2, 1890 – Nov. 16, 1907 | **Oklahoma Territory** (west) | Territorial courts, land offices, county clerks |
| Pre-1907 (eastern OK) | **Indian Territory** (Five Civilized Tribes) | Tribal governments + Dawes Commission |
| Nov. 16, 1907 onward | State of Oklahoma | State and county records |

Records filed under "Oklahoma Territory" and "Indian Territory" are in separate repositories — searching only one will miss half the picture.

---

## Record Types, Collections & Repositories

### 🏠 Land & Homestead Records — Start Here

Land Run homestead files are the cornerstone record for this period. Each file typically contains the original application, **proof of settlement with named witnesses**, and the final patent. Rejected applications survive too and can contain family details.

- **FamilySearch — "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"** (Collection 1541872): 234,567 records, 117,283 images. Covers the full territorial period. [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)
  - ⚠️ Digitization level (indexed vs. browse-only) not reported by the collections tool — verify on FamilySearch directly.
- **BLM General Land Office Records** (glorecords.blm.gov): Searchable land patents and partial homestead records. Free, online. Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **NARA — Record Group 49 (General Land Office)**: Full homestead case files. Physical access in Washington, D.C., or order copies by request. Same source.

> **Tip:** Homestead proof notices were **legally required to be published in local newspapers** before a patent was issued — search territorial newspapers on Newspapers.com for your ancestor's name as an independent confirmation of the claim.

---

### 📊 Census Records

- **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census** ⭐: This is one of the **few surviving 1890 census records in the nation** — the national census was largely destroyed by fire, but Oklahoma Territory's special census survives. Held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society** (okhistory.org). This is a critical resource unique to this jurisdiction. Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **1900, 1910, 1920 Federal Censuses**: Fully available on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.
- **County-Level Tax Rolls (1890s)**: Document early settlers between federal censuses; held at county courthouses and the **Oklahoma State Archives**. Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **FamilySearch — "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** (Collection 1987432): 567,890 records, 283,945 images. Essential for any family connected to the Five Civilized Tribes or living in Indian Territory. [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)

---

### ⚖️ Territorial Court Records (1890–1907)

Held at two repositories per wiki_search ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)):
- **NARA at Fort Worth** — the regional NARA facility for Oklahoma
- **Oklahoma State Archives**

Contents include district court civil and criminal cases, **probate records**, and critically — **naturalization records**. Pre-1906 naturalizations occurred in any court of record, meaning immigrant Land Run settlers were naturalized through these territorial courts, not federal courts.

---

### 💍 Vital Records

**Marriages:** "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (Collection 2134789): 456,789 records (913,578 persons), 228,394 images — begins 1890, covering the entire territorial and early statehood era. [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789)

**Births & Deaths:** Oklahoma had no statewide civil birth/death registration before statehood (1907). For the 1889–1907 period, **church records and county-level records** are the primary substitutes where they survive. See the FamilySearch Wiki vital records category: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Category:Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Category:Vital_Records)

---

### ⛪ Church & Mission Records

**FamilySearch — "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** (Collection 1654321): 123,456 records, 61,728 images. [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)

Mission records predate civil government and are especially important for Native American families and early settlers. Denominational congregations began forming sporadically from 1889 onward and are often the **only source for births and deaths** before statehood registration. Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

---

### 🎖️ Military Records

- **Fold3** (fold3.com): Civil War pension files, WWI draft registrations (1917–1918), service records. WWI draft cards document the children of Land Run settlers and are widely available.
- **NARA** (archives.gov): Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.

---

### 📰 Newspapers

- **Newspapers.com**: Historical newspapers including early territorial papers. Guthrie was the territorial capital and had active territorial-era papers.
- Beyond family news, territorial newspapers are a **legal record source**: homestead proof publication notices name the claimant, claim location, and witnesses — effectively an independent confirmation of the land file.

---

### 🪦 Cemetery Records

- **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com): Many pioneer Oklahoma cemeteries from the 1889–1910 era are indexed here.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Holdings Relevant to 1889–1920 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents, partial homestead records | Free online |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Homestead files (RG 49), territorial courts, military, naturalization | In-person / by request; some digitized |
| **NARA at Fort Worth** | Oklahoma territorial court records (RG 21), 1890–1907 | In-person |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (okhistory.org) | Surviving 1890 territorial census, early territorial records | In-person + some online |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** | Territorial courts, county records, state records | In-person |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | 4 confirmed collections: early land, Indian rolls, marriages, church | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses (1900, 1910, 1920) | Subscription |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Military records, pension files, WWI draft cards | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Territorial and early state newspapers incl. homestead notices | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |

---

## Key Research Strategies

1. **Oklahoma Territory vs. Indian Territory first.** Identify which side of the line your ancestor was on — it determines whether you search BLM/territorial courts vs. Dawes Commission/tribal rolls. Many eastern Oklahoma families appear in the Indian Censuses and Rolls collection (1987432) regardless of blood quantum.

2. **The 1890 census is not entirely gone for Oklahoma.** The Oklahoma Territory special census is a major exception to the national 1890 loss — check it at the Oklahoma Historical Society before assuming there's no 1890 record.

3. **Homestead files are people-rich.** Proof-of-settlement documents name neighbors as witnesses — these build your ancestor's social network and can identify relatives who settled nearby.

4. **Trace backwards to departure states.** Land Run settlers arrived heavily from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri (per wiki_search). Once you've located a settler in Oklahoma, search those states' records to extend the pedigree. Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

5. **Subsequent land runs (1891–1895) opened more land.** If your family isn't in 1889 records, check the later runs — each generated its own set of homestead files at NARA.

6. **Naturalization records are in territorial courts, not federal courts** before 1906 — look to NARA Fort Worth, not federal district court records, for immigrant settlers from this era.

---

## Coverage Gaps

- **FamilySearch wiki (Oklahoma-specific):** All four wiki_place_page sections returned generic fallback content, not an Oklahoma-specific page. For current, detailed wiki guidance, visit [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy) directly.
- **Volume search not available** in this environment — there may be additional digitized but unindexed browse-only image volumes for Oklahoma not surfaced above. Check the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) for Oklahoma browse volumes.
- **Digitization levels** (indexed vs. browse-only) were not returned for the four FamilySearch collections — verify on each collection page before planning your search strategy.
- **Population data** for Oklahoma returned no results from the population tool.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (c. 1780–1819) — Pre-Statehood Territorial Period

## Jurisdiction Overview

The region that became Alabama passed through four distinct governmental regimes before statehood, each generating its own record system:

| Period | Governing authority | Implications for records |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French colonial (Mobile District) | French sacramental & administrative records |
| 1763–1780 | British colonial | British land grants, church records |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish colonial (Mobile District) | Spanish census, church, and land records |
| 1798–1817 | U.S. Mississippi Territory | American territorial census, land, court records |
| 1817–1819 | U.S. Alabama Territory | Brief transitional period before statehood Dec. 14, 1819 |

**The territory was sparsely settled around 1800.** The first significant American settlement was in the Tombigbee River valley and the Mobile Bay area. Migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia accelerated dramatically after the Creek War of 1813–1814. The Creek and Cherokee nations inhabited the interior and were not subject to American civil records systems in this period.
*(Source: Wikipedia: [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama))*

---

## Boundary Changes — Critical for Research

This is the single most important research complication for this period. You must track **county formation** to know where records were filed:

- **Washington County** (est. 1800) covered nearly all of present-day Alabama at the start of the century. Most early American territorial records for the Alabama portion were created here.
- **Baldwin County** (1809), **Madison County** (1808), and **Mobile County** (1812) were carved from Washington County as settlement spread.
- Before any of these American counties existed, the region was administered through the older **Adams and Pickering counties** (est. 1799, in the Mississippi portion of the territory).

**The key research rule:** Records created before a given county existed are held by its parent county. For most of present-day Alabama around 1800, that parent is **Washington County**, whose records are the foundation of any territorial-era search.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Mississippi Territory Genealogy — County Formation," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Counties](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Counties))*

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births or deaths existed in the territorial period. Alabama did not begin statewide vital registration until **1908** — nearly a full century after your target date.
- **Marriages:** County-level marriage bonds and licenses began when each county formed (Washington County from ~1800, others from 1808–1812). These are the only "civil" vital records for 1800–1819.
- **Where held:** Original marriage records are at the respective county courthouses. FamilySearch has the collection **"Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** (collection ID 1598408; 612,345 indexed records, 306,172 images) — the 1809 start date reflects the earliest surviving county records that overlap with the pre-statehood window. **Digitization level: Indexed + images** for the portion starting 1809. Pre-1809 marriage records (Washington County, 1800–1808) are not in this collection and must be sought at physical repositories.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** See Church Records below.

### Church Records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist circuit riders and Baptist congregations arrived with the first American settlers. Catholic parishes were well established in the Mobile area from the French period. Presbyterian missionaries were active by the early 1800s.
- **Mobile area:** Spanish-era **Catholic parish registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) survive for the Mobile District from 1780 to 1813 and are among the richest records for the period. These are discussed further under Colonial Records below.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** (collection ID 1986396; 156,789 indexed records, 78,394 images). The 1803 start date means this collection does cover the last years of the territorial period. **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Physical repositories:** Local Baptist and Methodist association minutes from this era are scattered across church archives and the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery.

### Census Records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census covering the Alabama portion is **1810** (as part of Mississippi Territory). The 1800 federal census did not enumerate this region systematically. The 1820 federal census was the first taken after Alabama statehood.
- **Territorial censuses (highest priority for c. 1800):** The Mississippi Territory conducted enumerations in **1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816**. These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery and the **Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH)** in Jackson. These are not online on FamilySearch but are partially indexed in published transcriptions held by ADAH and genealogical societies.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** (collection ID 2016756; 287,634 indexed records, **no images**). This is a **name index only** — no images. Covers the 1810 federal census (earliest in Alabama) and tax-list substitutes. **Digitization level: Index only, no images.**
- **Mississippi Territory compilations:** The FamilySearch collection **"Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890"** (collection ID 1927171; 198,340 records, **no images**) covers the territorial period and may include enumerations for the Alabama portion of the territory. **Digitization level: Index only, no images.**
- *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))*

### Land Records — **Best-Documented Record Class for This Period**

Land is where this era is best served, for two reasons: federal land sales began almost immediately, and colonial-era grants were adjudicated by American authorities.

- **Federal land patents (1803 onward):** The U.S. government began selling public land in the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory through two land offices: **St. Stephens** (southern Alabama) and **Huntsville** (northern Alabama). Original land entry files are in **NARA Record Group 49** and fully indexed on the **BLM General Land Office (GLO) website** at [https://glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — **free, searchable by name, with document images**. This is the single most accessible digitized record source for the period. **Digitization level: Indexed + images (BLM GLO).**
- **Mississippi Territory land records:** FamilySearch collection **"Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907"** (collection ID 1919694; 312,450 indexed records, 156,225 images). This collection was filed under Mississippi at the collection level but covers the full territorial period including the Alabama portion. **Digitization level: Indexed + images.** This collection is your primary FamilySearch land resource for 1798–1817.
- **Colonial-era grants:** Spanish and British land grants in the Mobile District were confirmed (or challenged) by American authorities after 1813. Case files are at NARA and the Alabama State Archives. British grants (1763–1780) are in British colonial records, partly available through archives.
- **County deed books:** After county formation, deeds were recorded at the county courthouse. Washington County deed books from c. 1800 are the earliest American-era county land records for the Alabama interior.
- **Land system:** Alabama is a **federal land state** using the rectangular survey system (townships and ranges) for post-1803 entries.

### Probate and Court Records
- **Territorial courts:** The Mississippi Territory established district courts that handled probate, civil, and criminal matters. After county formation, county courts took over local probate.
- **FamilySearch collection (Alabama):** **"Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** (collection ID 1598408; 438,210 indexed records, 219,105 images). The 1809 start reflects the earliest surviving Alabama county probate material that has been digitized. **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **FamilySearch collection (Mississippi Territory):** **"Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920"** (collection ID 1855293; 245,670 indexed records, 122,835 images). This covers the territorial period and may include records for the Alabama portion of the territory filed under early Mississippi Territory counties. **Digitization level: Indexed + images.**
- **Washington County, AL courthouse:** Pre-statehood court and probate originals for the Alabama portion are held at the Washington County courthouse in Chatom, AL, and at ADAH.

### Colonial Records (Mobile District) — **Key Source for the Coastal Area**

If your research touches the Mobile area, these records pre-date American governance and are uniquely valuable:

- **French period (1702–1763):** Church records and administrative documents. Held at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm copies at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**. **Digitization level: Microfilm / physical only** (not online as of this survey).
- **Spanish period (1780–1813):** Census returns, Catholic church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials), and land grants for the Mobile District. Original records at the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, Spain, with partial copies at the **Library of Congress** in Washington, D.C. **Digitization level: Physical/microfilm at LoC** — not browsable online. Church registers may also be at the **Catholic Diocese of Mobile** archives.
- **British period (1763–1780):** British land grants and some church records. Available through British colonial archives; some are accessible via the UK National Archives.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))*

### Military Records
- **Creek War (1813–1814):** The most significant military event of the pre-statehood period. Militia service records and pension applications for Creek War service are at **NARA** and accessible through **Fold3** ([https://www.fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) (subscription). Pension files (under the 1818 and 1832 pension acts) contain biographical detail on veterans and their families. **Digitization level: Indexed + images (Fold3/Ancestry).**
- **War of 1812:** Some Alabama Territory men served. Records at NARA; searchable via Fold3.
- **Territorial militia rolls:** Partial militia muster rolls for the Mississippi Territory are held at ADAH and MDAH; these are not comprehensively digitized or indexed online.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))*

### Tax Records
- **What they are:** Territorial and early county tax lists (property and poll tax) were created annually and are the best substitute for the missing 1800 census and for years between territorial enumerations.
- **Where held:** ADAH (Montgomery) holds many surviving territorial tax lists. Some have been published or transcribed by the Alabama Genealogical Society.
- **Digitization level:** Not comprehensively digitized online. The "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (collection 2016756 on FamilySearch) incorporates some tax list data, but the underlying images are not available — index only.

### Newspaper Records
- **Coverage:** The first Alabama-area newspaper, the *Mobile Centinel*, appeared in 1811. Huntsville had a paper by 1816. Coverage for c. 1800 is essentially nonexistent in print.
- **Where held:** The **Alabama Department of Archives and History** holds microfilm of early Alabama newspapers. **Newspapers.com** and the **Chronicling America** project at the Library of Congress ([https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)) have some early Alabama titles, but coverage before 1819 is sparse.
- **Digitization level:** Very limited for the target period.

### Cemetery Records
- **Online coverage:** **FindAGrave** ([https://www.findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) has volunteer-transcribed entries for Alabama cemeteries, but coverage of early 19th-century graves (which were often unmarked fieldstones) is inconsistent.
- **Note:** Formal cemetery record-keeping did not exist in this period. Family and church burial grounds were the norm; few have surviving sexton records.

---

## Digitized, Browsable Volumes — Direct Answer to Your Question

You specifically asked about digitized, browsable volumes. Here is the honest answer from the tool data:

> **`volume_search` returned zero results for Alabama in the pre-statehood window (1780–1819), even with the date range expanded to 1800–1830.** FamilySearch has not catalogued any stand-alone digitized image volumes (browse-only or otherwise) tagged to Alabama for this period.

What *does* exist online with images:

| Source | What you can browse | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **BLM GLO website** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) | Federal land patents from Alabama land offices, 1803+. Name-searchable with patent images. | Free |
| **FamilySearch: Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907** (ID 1919694) | 156,225 images of territorial land records including Alabama portion; name-indexed | Free |
| **FamilySearch: Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920** (ID 1855293) | 122,835 images; covers territorial period; name-indexed | Free |
| **FamilySearch: Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (ID 1598408) | 306,172 images; indexed; earliest entries 1809 | Free |
| **FamilySearch: Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985** (ID 1537764) | 219,105 images; indexed; earliest entries 1809 | Free |
| **FamilySearch: Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950** (ID 1986396) | 78,394 images; indexed; earliest entries 1803 | Free |

For un-indexed browsable volumes, the territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, 1816) and tax lists must be consulted **in person or by request** at ADAH or MDAH — they have not been placed online as image volumes.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What's there for this period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Mississippi territorial land & court records 1798+; Alabama marriage/probate/church records from 1803–1809; census substitutes index | Free |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from Alabama land offices, 1803+ | Free |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Creek War and War of 1812 service records; pension files | Subscription |
| **Ancestry** (ancestry.com) | Federal census 1810+; some overlapping collections | Subscription |
| **Chronicling America** (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) | Early Alabama newspapers (sparse before 1819) | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History (ADAH)**, Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses 1801–1816; tax lists; militia rolls; early county records | In-person; some on microfilm |
| **Mississippi Dept. of Archives & History (MDAH)**, Jackson, MS | Mississippi Territory records including Alabama portion; territorial court files | In-person; some on microfilm |
| **National Archives (NARA)**, Washington, D.C. | Federal land entry files (RG 49); military service & pension records | In-person; some digitized via Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Washington County Courthouse**, Chatom, AL | Original deed books, court minutes, probate files from c. 1800 | In-person / mail |
| **Catholic Diocese of Mobile Archives** | Catholic parish registers for Mobile area, Spanish period onward | Contact archives |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C. | Copies of Spanish colonial records from the Archivo General de Indias | In-person |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives**, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French colonial church records | In-person |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France | Original French colonial records 1702–1763 | In-person / correspondence |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following record classes exist but have **not** been placed in any online database:

- **Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, 1816)** — at ADAH and MDAH; no online image set
- **Territorial militia rolls** — at ADAH and MDAH; partially transcribed in published volumes
- **Washington County early deed books (c. 1800–1808)** — at the courthouse; not digitized
- **Spanish colonial records of the Mobile District** — at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and the Library of Congress; not available online
- **French colonial church registers** — at ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) and Mobile Municipal Archives; not available online

---

## Known Record Losses and Gaps

- **Very thin coverage before 1798:** Outside the Mobile coastal area, there are essentially no surviving European-American records for the Alabama interior before American territorial government began.
- **Washington County early records:** Some early Washington County records were damaged or lost. Researchers should check both ADAH and the courthouse for survival status.
- **No statewide vital registration until 1908:** There is a 90-year gap between statehood and civil registration. Church records, county marriage bonds, and probate records are the only substitutes.
- **Creek and Cherokee nations:** Individuals of Native heritage are largely absent from American civil records of this period. Tribal records and later Dawes Rolls era materials require a separate research strategy.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the Mississippi Territory, not Alabama.** Around 1800, the jurisdiction is the Mississippi Territory. Search FamilySearch's Mississippi collections (land records ID 1919694; court records ID 1855293) for people who lived in what is now Alabama — they were legally Mississippians at the time.

2. **Track county of residence year by year.** A family living near Huntsville in 1808 was in Madison County (just formed); the same family in 1804 was in Washington County. Search the correct county for each year or you will miss records entirely.
   *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Counties](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Counties))*

3. **BLM GLO is your best freely browsable source.** If your ancestor arrived in Alabama before 1819, they almost certainly acquired land. The BLM GLO site ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) is free, name-searchable, and shows the original patent with the exact legal description and date — a foundation document for any territorial-era family.

4. **Mobile-area research requires a colonial-era strategy.** If your family was in the Mobile Bay area, the most informative records may be Spanish Catholic registers (baptisms, marriages, burials through 1813). Contact the **Catholic Diocese of Mobile** and check for microfilm at the Family History Library in Salt Lake City before assuming no records exist.

5. **Territorial censuses beat the 1810 federal census for detail.** The 1801, 1805, 1808 territorial enumerations predate the first federal census of this region and name heads of household. Write to ADAH (Montgomery) for access or look for published transcriptions through the **Alabama Genealogical Society** (alabamagenealogy.org).

6. **Creek War pension files are a genealogical gold mine.** Veterans who served in 1813–1814 could apply for pensions under the 1818 and 1832 pension acts. These files, held at NARA and available on Fold3, often contain birthplaces, ages, family members, and migration histories — invaluable for reconstructing early Alabama families.

7. **No browsable image volumes on FamilySearch for this period.** `volume_search` returned zero results for Alabama pre-1820. The digitized collections that exist (IDs above) are name-indexed, not browse-only volumes. If you want to page through original documents, your path leads to ADAH, MDAH, or the county courthouse — not FamilySearch's image viewer.
