# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)
**Counties: Schuylkill · Carbon · Luzerne · Lackawanna · Northumberland**
*Focus: Irish immigrant mining families*

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

| County | Formed | From | County Seat |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Schuylkill** | 1811 | Berks + Northampton | Pottsville |
| **Carbon** | 1843 | Monroe + Northampton | Jim Thorpe (Mauch Chunk) |
| **Luzerne** | 1786 | Northumberland | Wilkes-Barre |
| **Lackawanna** | 1878 | Luzerne | Scranton |
| **Northumberland** | 1772 | Lancaster + Bedford + Cumberland + Berks + Northampton | Sunbury |

**Population (Schuylkill County — the best-documented coal county via tools):**
60,713 (1850) → **89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880)** → 172,927 (1900). The population tool characterizes this as "rapid growth driven by anthracite coal mining; large immigrant population (Irish, Welsh, German, later Eastern European) from 1840s onward."

**Ethnic composition:** Irish dominated the unskilled and semi-skilled mine labor force, many arriving via Philadelphia after the Great Famine. Welsh miners held higher-skilled positions (hoisting engineers, fire bosses). German settlers were present in Schuylkill and Carbon from the colonial era. Eastern European workers (Slovak, Lithuanian, Polish) arrived in the later 1880s–1890s.

**Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish and German parishes), Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Methodist Episcopal, Episcopal, Lutheran, Presbyterian.

**Key events:** Workingmen's Benevolent Association Long Strike (1875); Molly Maguires trials, Pottsville (1876–1878); establishment of Diocese of Scranton (1868); Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company consolidation of the Schuylkill fields.

---

## Boundary Changes

> ⚠️ **The single most important boundary fact for this region:**

- **Lackawanna County did not exist until 1878.** It was carved from Luzerne County. All records for Scranton and surrounding townships before 1878 were created under **Luzerne County**. Researchers unfamiliar with this split routinely miss pre-1878 records for Scranton-area ancestors — search Luzerne County first for any event before 1878.
- **Carbon County** records before 1843 are in Monroe and Northampton counties.
- **Schuylkill County** records before 1811 are in Berks and Northampton counties (confirmed by `place_search_all`).
- **Luzerne County** records before 1786 are in Northumberland County.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

Pennsylvania's civil registration history has a **critical gap** for the 1860–1890 window:

- Pennsylvania passed a statewide vital registration law in **1852**, but compliance in the coal counties was extremely poor. The FamilySearch wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy) confirms researchers must check specific start dates before assuming records exist, and that many U.S. states did not achieve effective statewide registration until the early 1900s.
- **Deaths:** A county-level death registration requirement was enacted in **1893**. Statewide reliable registration of births and deaths did not begin until **1906**.
- **Marriage licenses:** County-level and more consistently kept. FamilySearch volume search found Schuylkill County marriage records 1870–1910 (imageGroupNumber 007936753, 94 images): **browse-only, 0% name-indexed.**

**Practical consequence:** For 1860–1890 births and deaths, do not rely on civil vital records. **Church records are the primary substitute** for this entire period.

- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg); county Register of Wills offices.

---

### Church Records ⭐ *Primary vital record substitute for Irish Catholics*

This is the **most important record class** for Irish Catholic miners throughout the 1860–1890 period.

- **Roman Catholic parishes:** Irish miners were overwhelmingly Catholic. The **Diocese of Scranton** (established 1868) covers Lackawanna, Luzerne, and adjoining northern anthracite counties. **Carbon and Schuylkill counties** fall under the Diocese of Allentown (originally part of the Diocese of Philadelphia). Parish registers record baptisms, marriages, and burials — the effective vital registration for the Irish community.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** [Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1401638) (collection ID 1401638): **1,245,830 records · 982,415 persons · 607,220 images.** This is name-indexed and searchable — the best starting point.
- **FamilySearch Schuylkill County browse-only volume:** Church Records 1842–1895 (imageGroupNumber 007936751, 187 images): **0% name-indexed, browse-only. Languages: English and German.** German-language entries require reading German script (some Catholic parishes served German-speaking miners alongside Irish).
- **Other denominations:** Welsh Calvinist Methodist churches in the anthracite region kept registers in Welsh and English. Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian, and Episcopal parish registers survive at varying rates.
- **Physical repositories:** Diocese of Scranton Archives (Scranton, PA); Diocese of Allentown Archives; local parishes; Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville).

---

### Census Records

| Census Year | Status | Key Value |
|---|---|---|
| 1860 | Indexed + images (FamilySearch, Ancestry) | Birthplace; lists all household members |
| 1870 | Indexed + images | Birthplace; naturalization status |
| 1880 | Indexed + images | **First to show relationship to head of household** — most valuable for proving family structure |
| **1890** | ⚠️ **Nearly entirely destroyed** | Population schedules lost nationwide (1921 fire); veterans' schedules only survive for some counties |
| 1900 | Indexed + images | Year of immigration; years in U.S.; mother's name; lists all children |

- **The 1900 census bridges the 1890 gap** — it captures year of immigration, years married, and parent birthplaces, making it the most genealogically rich census for Irish immigrant families.
- **Mortality Schedules 1850–1880:** Record deaths in the year preceding each census; available for Pennsylvania; indexed on Ancestry. Useful substitute for missing death records.
- **Pennsylvania conducted no state census** between federal enumerations — there is no PA state census to fill the 1890 gap.
- Source for census facts: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records

---

### Naturalization Records ⭐ *Often the only document naming the Irish county of origin*

- **Pre-September 27, 1906:** Declarations of intent ("first papers") and petitions ("second papers") could be filed in **any court of record.** In the coal counties this means Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts at the county level — search all three, not just one. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records)
- **Post-September 27, 1906:** Naturalization centralized in federal courts. Eastern Pennsylvania records are at **NARA Philadelphia** (Mid-Atlantic region).
- **FamilySearch Schuylkill County volume:** Naturalization Records 1849–1915 (imageGroupNumber 007936750, 298 images): **0% name-indexed, browse-only.** Must be browsed page by page.
- **Strategy tip:** Use the 1870, 1880, and 1900 census "naturalized/alien" column to estimate when your ancestor naturalized, then target that approximate year range in the browse-only volume. The 1900 census also records years of residency.

---

### Probate Records

- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) (collection ID 1999196): **2,304,118 records and images.**
- **FamilySearch Schuylkill County volume:** Probate Records 1851–1930 (imageGroupNumber 007936749, 412 images): **0% name-indexed, browse-only.**
- **Value:** Wills name heirs and sometimes siblings or relatives still in Ireland. Guardianship files name minor children and establish parent-child relationships when vital records are absent.
- **Where held:** County Register of Wills (county courthouses); Pennsylvania State Archives microfilm copies.

---

### Land and Deed Records

- **FamilySearch Schuylkill County volume:** Deed Records 1815–1900 (imageGroupNumber 007936752, 543 images): **22% name-indexed** — the only partially indexed county-level volume for Schuylkill. Images viewable online.
- **Practical note:** The majority of Irish mine laborers rented company housing from the colliery operator and did not own land. Deed records are more productive for mine operators, tradesmen, and farmers than for common miners — though some miners did acquire property after years in the region.
- **Where held:** County Recorder of Deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives microfilm.

---

### Mining and Occupational Records ⭐ *Unique to the coal region — high priority*

This class of records exists nowhere else and should be worked alongside standard genealogical sources.

- **Colliery employment and payroll records:** Where they survive, these list worker names, nationalities, and sometimes prior residence. The **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) holds payroll ledgers for several collieries. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Coal_Mining_Records)
- **Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines annual reports:** Published from 1870 onward; list mine names, operators, workforce counts, and — after accidents — **names of killed and injured miners.** Available at the Pennsylvania State Archives and many libraries; physical/microfilm only, not online.
- **Mine accident coroner's inquests:** Filed at the county courthouse; often provide age, birthplace (Ireland), and next of kin for deceased miners.
- **Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company records:** Held at the **Hagley Museum and Library** (Wilmington, DE). The P&R was the dominant operator in Schuylkill County. Employment records, payrolls, and administrative files. In-person research required.
- **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton, PA): Records pertaining to the Luzerne/Lackawanna coal fields.
- **Digitization status:** Not indexed or available on FamilySearch or Ancestry — physical repositories only.

---

### Molly Maguires Court Records ⭐ *Specialized index for Schuylkill County Irish*

- Active among Irish miners in Schuylkill County in the 1860s–1870s, the Molly Maguires trials (1876–1878) generated **trial transcripts, depositions, and Pinkerton detective agency reports naming hundreds of Irish-born miners and their families.** Some records identify specific counties of origin in Ireland (particularly County Donegal, Mayo, and Galway). (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires)
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse (Pottsville); Historical Society of Schuylkill County; Pennsylvania State Archives; portions published and transcribed.
- **Pinkerton reports** (James McParland's undercover reports) have been partially published in scholarly works and are held at various archives.
- Even if your ancestor was not a Molly Maguire, the extensive newspaper coverage and trial documents named countless Irish miners as witnesses, neighbors, and community members.

---

### Military Records

- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Many Irish miners served in Pennsylvania regiments.
  - Compiled Military Service Records (CMSRs): Fold3/Ancestry (subscription) or NARA request
  - Pension files at NARA: can name birthplace in Ireland, widow, children — genealogically rich
  - Pennsylvania Civil War veterans' card file: Pennsylvania State Archives
- **1863 Civil War Draft Registration (Provost Marshal):** Covers all men ages 20–45 in the coal counties. Schuylkill County had significant draft resistance. Records are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Veterans' Schedules of the 1890 Census:** The only 1890 census fragment to survive; lists Civil War veterans with disability information.

---

### Newspapers

| Paper | Location | Period | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Miners' Journal* | Pottsville (Schuylkill) | 1825–present | Mine accidents, labor disputes, Irish community news, Molly Maguires coverage |
| *Scranton Republican* / *Scranton Tribune* | Scranton (Lackawanna) | 1860s onward | Obituaries, naturalization notices, labor news |
| *Wilkes-Barre Record* / *Wilkes-Barre Times* | Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne) | 1860s onward | Same |
| *Hazleton Sentinel* | Hazleton (Luzerne/Carbon) | 1860s onward | Southern fields coverage |

- **Access:** Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free) covers some PA papers; Newspapers.com and Genealogy Bank (subscription); physical microfilm at local libraries and Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **The *Miners' Journal*** is the essential coal-region newspaper — it named participants in accidents, strikes, and trials and is especially useful for identifying Irish miners.

---

### Immigration Records

- **Primary ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden pre-1892; Ellis Island 1892–).
- **Passenger lists:** Indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch for Philadelphia (1800–1882) and New York (1820–) arrivals.
- **Content warning:** Pre-1895 manifests typically record only "Ireland" as birthplace — specific county/townland of origin rarely appears until post-1895 manifests and is most detailed post-1906. To identify the Irish parish, use naturalization records (post-1906), chain migration research among neighbors, and DNA.
- **Full manifest strategy:** Examine the full ship manifest — infants and children are listed with parents.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Key collections for this region | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records 1708–1985 (col. 1401638, 1.2M records); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (col. 1999196, 2.3M images); Schuylkill County volumes (naturalization 1849–1915; deed records 1815–1900; church records 1842–1895; marriage records 1870–1910; probate 1851–1930) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census 1860–1940; PA naturalization databases; 1863 Civil War draft; military (Fold3); Pennsylvania newspapers | Subscription |
| **NARA / Fold3** | Civil War CMSRs, pension files; post-1906 naturalization (NARA Philadelphia) | Subscription / Free at NARA |
| **Chronicling America** | *Miners' Journal* and other PA papers | Free |
| **FindAGrave** | Catholic and Protestant cemeteries throughout coal region | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Post-1906 vital records; county deed/probate microfilm; Civil War veterans' files; Bureau of Mines reports | In-person or online request |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville) | Colliery payroll ledgers; local newspapers; Molly Maguires materials; county records | In-person |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives (Scranton) | Catholic parish registers for Lackawanna, Luzerne, and surrounding counties | In-person or written request |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill and Carbon counties | In-person or written request |
| Hagley Museum & Library (Wilmington, DE) | Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company employment, payroll, and administrative records | In-person |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) | Coal company records, photographs, labor history for northern anthracite fields | In-person |
| County courthouses (Pottsville, Jim Thorpe, Wilkes-Barre, Scranton, Sunbury) | Deed books, probate files, naturalization records, Quarter Sessions/Common Pleas case files | In-person |
| NARA Philadelphia | Post-1906 federal court naturalization records for eastern Pennsylvania | In-person or records request |

---

## Records NOT Online

These exist but are **not in any online database:**

- Colliery employment and payroll records (Hagley, Historical Society of Schuylkill County)
- Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines annual accident reports with worker-level data (PA State Archives)
- Coroner's inquest records for mine accident deaths (county courthouses)
- Most pre-1906 Catholic parish registers for Lackawanna, Luzerne, and Carbon counties (diocesan archives)
- County tax assessment records 1860–1890 (county archives)
- Molly Maguires trial transcripts and Pinkerton detective reports (originals at Schuylkill County Courthouse; partial transcriptions published)
- Most Quarter Sessions and Common Pleas court records (county courthouses, physical only)
- **Schuylkill County naturalization records 1849–1915** (vol. 007936750) — digitized but **0% indexed; browse-only** — not discoverable by name search

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1890 U.S. Federal Census:** Population schedules for Pennsylvania are almost entirely destroyed (1921 Washington D.C. fire). Only veterans' schedules survive for some counties. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records
- **Lackawanna County records before 1878:** Not destroyed — but filed under Luzerne County. Researchers unfamiliar with this boundary change will fail to find pre-1878 Scranton-area events.
- **Civil vital records 1860–1893:** Pennsylvania had no reliably enforced civil vital registration during most of the target period. Church records are the substitute; their absence in a given parish represents a true documentation gap.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with 1880, then 1900, skipping the destroyed 1890.** The 1880 census first records family relationships; the 1900 census captures year of immigration and years of U.S. residence, bridging the 1890 gap.

2. **Lackawanna = Luzerne before 1878.** Any Scranton-area ancestor event before 1878 is in Luzerne County records. Search Luzerne County first.

3. **Naturalization records before 1906 are browse-only in this region.** The Schuylkill County naturalization volume (007936750) is 0% indexed. Use census records (1870/1880/1900 ask alien/naturalized status) to narrow the window, then browse the images.

4. **Search all three courts for naturalizations.** Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, and Orphans' Courts in each county all had naturalization authority pre-1906. A negative in one does not mean absent from the others. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records)

5. **Molly Maguires records name hundreds of Irish miners.** Trial transcripts, depositions, and Pinkerton reports document Irish-born miners in Schuylkill County in the 1860s–1870s with names, ages, and sometimes Irish county of origin. Even non-participants appear as witnesses and neighbors. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires)

6. **Colliery payroll records can identify Irish origin.** The Historical Society of Schuylkill County holds payroll ledgers for several collieries listing worker names, nationalities, and sometimes prior residence. Not online — contact the Society directly. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Coal_Mining_Records)

7. **Church records are the primary vital record.** Catholic parishes were established in coal towns from the 1840s onward. Begin with the indexed FamilySearch collection 1401638 (Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records 1708–1985), then contact the diocesan archives.

8. **Some Schuylkill church records are in German.** Volume 007936751 (1842–1895) is in both English and German — German-speaking Catholic parishes served miners of both ethnicities; don't assume all Catholic registers are in English.

9. **The *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville) is an essential finding aid.** It systematically covered mine accidents (naming the deceased and their nationalities), labor disputes, and court proceedings. Available on Chronicling America (free) and Newspapers.com (subscription).

10. **Chain migration — work the FAN club.** Many coal-region Irish emigrated in groups from the same townland or parish. When you hit a documentation wall on Irish origins, research your ancestor's mining neighbors and associates — their naturalization records or obituaries may name the same Irish parish.

---

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, c. 1750–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Status during period:** Not yet a U.S. state. Vermont passed through three successive regimes of authority before admission as the 14th state on March 4, 1791.
- **Administrative center:** No permanent capital existed during the Republic of Vermont period; the legislature rotated among towns (Windsor, Bennington, Middlebury, Newbury, and others).
- **Population:** The population data tool returned no figures for Vermont before 1800 in this environment. Vermont's first federal census (1790) recorded approximately 85,000 persons.
- **Economy:** Subsistence and small-scale commercial agriculture, logging, potash production, early river-mill industries.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly settlers of English descent migrating from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire; some Scots-Irish; Abenaki peoples, who had occupied the territory long before European settlement.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist churches were established earliest; Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal, and Quaker congregations followed.
- **Key events:** New Hampshire Grants dispute (1749–1777); French and Indian War raids; Vermont Declaration of Independence (1777); Battle of Bennington (1777); Republic of Vermont (1777–1791); Revolutionary War frontier raids along the Connecticut River valley and Lake Champlain corridor.

---

## Boundary changes — the most critical complexity for this period

Three successive authority claims produced records in *three different jurisdictions*, all covering the same physical territory:

| Period | Governing authority | Where records were made |
|---|---|---|
| 1749–1764 | **New Hampshire** (Benning Wentworth grants) | New Hampshire State Archives |
| 1764–1781 | **New York** (Crown ruling, 1764; NY imposed its own county structure) | New York State Archives and NY county repositories |
| 1777–1791 | **Republic of Vermont** (independent; created its own counties beginning 1778) | Vermont State Archives and Vermont county repositories |

The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) underscores this directly: *"Vermont, the 14th state (admitted 1791), has a distinctive set of pre-statehood land records that researchers should not confuse with later post-statehood records."*

**Practical consequence:** A family living in present-day Windsor County in 1772 appears in *New York* county records (Cumberland or Gloucester County, NY) — not Vermont records. Always work backward through all three authority layers, not just Vermont repositories.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Statewide registration start:** **1857** — documented in the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page. This is entirely outside the pre-statehood period.
- **Town-level records:** The wiki states: *"Earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly."* There was no statewide registration requirement during the Republic of Vermont era.
- **Level of access:** Town clerk offices hold original records; some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch (search the FamilySearch Catalog by Vermont town). Survival and indexing vary widely by town. **Physical or microfilm only** for most pre-1857 material.
- **Digitization status:** Specific digitized FamilySearch vital-records collections for Vermont pre-1800 could not be confirmed — `collections_search` and `volume_search` were not available in this environment. Consult the FamilySearch Catalog directly.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, family bibles, cemetery inscriptions, and town histories (see below).

### Church records

- The FamilySearch Vermont wiki page does not enumerate specific church collections or denominations for the pre-statehood period — that content was not returned by the wiki tools in this environment.
- **What to expect:** Congregational churches were the earliest established in most Vermont towns; Baptist and other dissenting congregations followed. Church registers (baptism, marriage, burial) are the primary alternative to absent civil registration.
- **Access:** Original registers held by individual congregations or successor churches; some held at denominational archives; some microfilmed by FamilySearch — search the FamilySearch Catalog by Vermont town to find what is available.
- **Digitization status:** Unknown in this environment; catalog search required.

### Census records

- **No federal census** existed during the pre-statehood period.
- **First federal census, 1790:** Taken immediately after statehood, this is the anchor enumeration for all pre-statehood Vermont families. It captures the population that was present during the Republic of Vermont years. Available indexed on Ancestry.com (listed as a FamilySearch-curated resource for this period) and on FamilySearch.
- **Republic of Vermont substitutes:** Tax lists and militia rolls from the 1777–1791 period serve a census-like function. Held at the Vermont State Archives. Specific digitized holdings were not confirmed by tools.
- **New York-era lists:** New York colonial tax and assessment lists for Cumberland and Gloucester counties (covering present Vermont territory, 1764–1781) are held at the New York State Archives and may enumerate Vermont settlers.

### Vital records — the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (prime pre-statehood source)

This record is specifically documented in the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page and is **the most important pre-statehood resident list available:**

> *"The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule, prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood, enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry lists grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This record predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state."*
> — FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy

This is your first stop for placing a family in pre-statehood Vermont territory.

### Probate and court records

- The tools returned no Vermont-specific content on probate records. Specific collections and their digitization status could not be confirmed.
- **What to expect:** Vermont probate courts were organized at the district level by the Republic of Vermont (some records begin in the early 1780s). Pre-Republic probate for Vermont settlers would be in New York county records (Cumberland or Gloucester counties, 1764–1781).
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) and Vermont county probate district offices. New York State Archives for the 1764–1781 NY-era records.
- **Access:** Search the FamilySearch Catalog by Vermont county for microfilmed probate holdings; contact Vermont State Archives for early district records.

### Land records

The FamilySearch Vermont wiki identifies land records as the defining pre-statehood record class. Three distinct layers must be worked together:

1. **New Hampshire Grants (1749–1764):** Original grants issued by NH Governor Benning Wentworth — held at the New Hampshire State Archives, and reprinted in published volumes of New Hampshire colonial records.
2. **New York colonial land records (1764–1781):** NY imposed its own grants over NH grantees. New York county records (Cumberland County, Gloucester County) for Vermont territory are at the New York State Archives.
3. **Vermont land records (1777–1791):** Town proprietors' records and land transfers recorded by town clerks under the Republic of Vermont. Held at individual town clerk offices and the Vermont State Archives.

**Town histories as a land-record surrogate:** The FamilySearch Vermont wiki page specifically notes: *"Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access."* Many are digitized on HathiTrust, Google Books, and the Internet Archive — freely accessible.

- **Digitization status of land records proper:** Not confirmed by tools. Search the FamilySearch Catalog by Vermont town/county.

### Military records

- **FamilySearch curated resources** for Vermont, 1750–1791 include **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) and **NARA** (https://www.archives.gov/) — both listed in the FamilySearch external links for this period and time window.
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Key records at NARA:** Revolutionary War service records, pension and bounty land warrant files — the primary federal source for this period. Some are indexed and digitized on Fold3 (subscription).
- **Vermont-specific:** The Vermont State Archives holds state-level militia records from the Republic of Vermont period.
- **Digitization status:** Revolutionary War pension files are extensively digitized on Fold3 and at Ancestry.com.

### Cemetery records

- **FindAGrave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) is listed as a FamilySearch-curated resource for Vermont cemetery records in this period.
- Many pre-statehood Vermont cemeteries are small family or town burial grounds established in the 1760s–1780s. Coverage on FindAGrave varies significantly by town.
- **Physical:** Sexton records and church burial registers for congregations established before 1791 may document burials. Access through individual churches or historical societies.

### Newspaper records

- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) is listed as a FamilySearch-curated resource for Vermont historical newspapers in this period.
- Vermont's earliest newspapers date from the 1780s: the *Vermont Gazette* (Bennington, 1781) and *Vermont Journal* (Windsor, 1783) are among the earliest. Coverage is sparse for the strictly pre-statehood years before ~1781.
- **Content value:** Land dispute notices, legal announcements, militia calls, and community notices appear in these papers. Obituaries and marriage notices are present but sparse in this era.

### Tax records

- Republic of Vermont tax lists from 1777–1791 survive and are held at the Vermont State Archives. These can substitute for missing census records before the 1790 federal census.
- Specific digitized holdings were not confirmed by the tools in this environment.

### Town histories (a primary source class for this period)

Explicitly documented in the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page as critical for pre-statehood research: *"Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access."*

These published volumes frequently contain: early settlers' lists, family genealogies, reprinted town meeting records, proprietors' records, and early vital entries. Many are freely searchable on **HathiTrust** (hathitrust.org) and **Internet Archive** (archive.org).

---

## Records NOT online (as of this survey)

The following record types are known to exist but specific digitized online collections **could not be confirmed** — `collections_search` and `volume_search` tools were not available in this environment:

- **Town clerk vital records, 1770s–1791:** Physical at individual town clerk offices; some microfilmed at FamilySearch — search FamilySearch Catalog by town
- **Republic of Vermont tax lists and militia rolls:** Vermont State Archives; not confirmed online
- **Vermont county probate records, 1780s–1791:** Vermont State Archives and county probate courts; not confirmed online
- **Town proprietors' records:** Town clerk offices; partially reprinted in published town histories (HathiTrust, Internet Archive)
- **New York colonial records for Vermont territory, 1764–1781:** New York State Archives; not confirmed online
- **New Hampshire grant records, 1749–1764:** New Hampshire State Archives; some reprinted in published NH colonial records volumes

**Action for each:** Search the FamilySearch Catalog at catalog.familysearch.org, filtering by Vermont county or town, to identify what has been microfilmed or digitized.

---

## Known record losses

The tools did not return Vermont-specific data on courthouse fires or record destructions. No major statewide record catastrophe is documented in the tool results. Note:

- Record survival is inherently uneven for the Republic of Vermont period — civil infrastructure was minimal and record-keeping was not yet standardized.
- The NH/NY land-title dispute means some early land records were contested, duplicated, or held across two sets of repositories (NH and NY); gaps in one may be partially compensated by the other.

---

## Research tips

*(Grounded in the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy — and the tool results above)*

1. **Start with the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.** It is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state (~1,800 entries), documents the NH/NY land-claim conflict, and may place your ancestor in a specific township before any other record does. It is specifically documented in the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki.

2. **Do not confuse pre-statehood and post-statehood records.** The FamilySearch wiki flags this explicitly. Land records span NH-grant, NY-colonial, Republic of Vermont, and US-state eras — each in a different repository. Check all three layers.

3. **Chase New York county records for the 1764–1781 window.** A family in present-day Windsor or Windham County in 1770 was officially in Cumberland or Gloucester County, New York. NY-era probate and court records for Vermont territory are at the New York State Archives, not Vermont.

4. **Town clerk records are the only vital-record source before 1857 at the state level.** Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1857 (documented in FamilySearch wiki). Town clerk offices hold records going back to the 1770s in some towns — but survival is uneven. Contact each town clerk directly.

5. **Mine 19th-century town histories aggressively.** The FamilySearch wiki specifically recommends them because they reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise hard to access. Search HathiTrust and Internet Archive by Vermont town name.

6. **Use the 1790 federal census as your anchor and work backward.** It is the first complete population enumeration and captures the pre-statehood generation in place. Cross-reference with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule and Republic-era tax lists to triangulate families.

7. **For Revolutionary War ancestors, use Fold3 and NARA.** Both are FamilySearch-curated resources for this period. Federal pension files often include depositions with biographical detail — names of spouses, children, places of residence — that substitute for absent vital records.

8. **Check the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page directly** at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy for fuller coverage of individual record types. The wiki tools in this research environment returned only the page's home-level content; the full wiki article addresses land, probate, church, and military records in more detail.
